articles.title: King tides bring record coastal flooding to California
articles.description: The highest coastal water levels in over a century of record-keeping occurred in both San Diego and Los Angeles today, beating the records set just last month.
paragraphs: The king tides of November clobbered California during the morning high tide on Nov. 25, bringing the highest coastal water levels in over a century of record-keeping to both San Diego and Los Angeles, beating records set just last month. Monterey also had its highest water level on record (since 1973), Santa Monica, its second-highest (since 1933); Point Reyes, its fourth-highest (since 1975); Alameda, its sixth-highest (since 1939); Humboldt, its fifth-highest (since 1977); and San Francisco, its ninth-highest (since 1897). Oregon also got into the act, with Charleston, located about 100 miles north of the California border, experiencing its second-highest water level on record (since 1970), and South Beach, its eighth-highest (since 1967). Of the top-10 water levels on record for California’s three largest coastal cities, 60% are now from 2026 (see yellow-highlighted entries in Fig. 1).

The high-water records occurred during weather usually unfavorable for setting such records: clear skies, light winds, and above-average surface pressures. But this week marks the arrival of the king tides, when the elliptical orbit of the moon brings it closest to the Earth, resulting in the highest tides of the year.

The other key factor: a very strong El Niño event that brought record-warm water to the coast, resulting in local sea level rise. Sea surface temperatures more than 5°C (9°F) above average are present along most of the California coast. That’s substantially boosting sea levels because water expands as it warms. And with the king tide and El Niño-driven warm water arriving at a time when human-caused sea level rise has substantially boosted water levels, we now have a recipe for record flooding in the absence of a storm.

While today marks the peak amplitude of the astronomical high tides from this king tide event, Thanksgiving Day water levels will also be very high, likely setting top-10 water level marks all along the California coast. In southern California, the flooding will be worsened by the arrival of a long-period west swell Wednesday night that will prevail into Thursday. In San Diego, this swell will generate large breaking waves of 6-8 feet on Thursday, with sets of 10-12 feet on exposed west-facing beaches. Santa Barbara is expecting breaking waves of 15-22 feet, and in Los Angeles and Malibu, 6-11 feet. A High Surf Advisory is in effect for most of Southern California.

While the tides will be gradually decreasing through next week, we need to keep an eye on a strong Pacific storm predicted to hit central California on Tuesday, Dec. 1. Models are predicting that this storm will bring strong southerly winds, very low surface pressures, and heavy rain to the coast – conditions ideal for generating a significant storm surge, as explained in my post Monday, What’s causing major coastal flooding in California?

We’re not done with king tides after this week: The December 23-25 and January 21-22 full moon periods will have king tides similar in magnitude to this week’s (see the Bluesky post by Daniel Swain below to see the timing and severity of the coastal flooding possible). With this winter’s El Niño event not yet at its peak, the record-warm water by the coast isn’t going anywhere soon, and may spread farther north to the coasts of Oregon, Washington, and British Columbia, increasing coastal flooding odds there.
articles.lede: The highest coastal water levels in over a century of record-keeping occurred in both San Diego and Los Angeles today, beating the records set just last month.

articles.title: The Guardian view on rising energy prices: only bold action can win public confidence
articles.description: Editorial: Andy Burnham needs a radical vision of economic change to move on from policies aimed at giving voters ‘breathing space’
paragraphs: A sk Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living. Responding to the results of midterm elections in the US earlier this month, he said that the Democratic party’s triumph meant that there was “an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that’s the cost of living”.

This wasn’t a non sequitur. The Republicans lost control of Congress in large part because Donald Trump failed to address concerns about the cost of basic goods – a failing aggravated by the US president’s disastrous war against Iran, which caused a spike in commodity prices, exacerbating the affordability problem.

Mr Burnham correctly identified the transmission mechanism by which geopolitical problems feed domestic political resentment. “I can’t get people’s cost of living pressures down until the conflict in the Middle East is resolved, the conflict in Ukraine started by Russia,” the prime minister said.

The truth of that observation was painfully clear on Wednesday, when Ofgem, the energy regulator, announced that the price cap applied on domestic bills would rise in January. That means around 22 million UK households will pay an average equivalent to £2,166 a year for gas and electricity, up from £1,723 under the current cap.

International conflict and the climate emergency are driving up costs for British homes. Gas supply has been made volatile by uncertainty in the strait of Hormuz, while European reserves were depleted by exceptional energy usage to mitigate the effects of the summer’s ferocious and prolonged heatwave.

That leaves the continent poorly resourced to face what might be an unusually cold winter caused by the disruption of the polar vortex, plausibly accelerated by anthropogenic climate change. Many British households will face painful choices between heating their homes and affording other essentials. That hardship will exhaust the cost of living “breathing space” already offered by Mr Burnham – a VAT cut to bills and a one-off £100 payment to some households.

Meanwhile, the Conservatives and Reform UK claim that high bills are a function of environmental policies and look for solutions in the abandonment of Britain’s commitments to net zero – an approach that combines economic illiteracy with international irresponsibility. A dash to get dwindling North Sea oil on to a global market where the price is determined more by Mr Trump’s caprices or Vladimir Putin’s territorial aggressions is no shortcut to cheaper British bills.

Hastening the transition away from fossil fuels is the strategic route to energy security and the stability that permits other interventions to help with the cost of living. That argument must be central to the analysis that Mr Burnham offers when he moves on from “breathing space” policies to the more ambitious vision promised in a 10-year plan.

The prime minister has advertised that document, due to be published next month, as a blueprint for fixing “broken” markets, and restoring public control over utilities and other services on which people depend. What that means in practice will decide the fate of the Labour government. His focus on the cost of living is the right one, given how quick voters are to punish incumbents who fail to appreciate the scale of the problem or are perceived to lack credible solutions. Mr Burnham has passed the first of those tests. He cannot afford to fail the second one.
articles.lede: A sk Andy Burnham a question and it won’t be long before he mentions the cost of living.

articles.title: Correct, The Economist, CO2 Deserves Most of the Credit for Africa’s Greening
articles.description: Africa is getting greener and water more plentiful. Formerly parched land is supporting more vegetation and lakes are refilling.
paragraphs: The Economist (TE) deserves credit for its article, “Climate change is making some African deserts greener,” which acknowledges that portions of Africa long predicted to suffer relentless desertification due to climate change are becoming wetter and greener, instead. It is refreshing to see a major publication acknowledge correctly that climate change and rising atmospheric carbon dioxide is produce benefits for plant life and ecosystems. Satellite observations have documented substantial greening across the planet for decades, and NASA has reported that rising atmospheric carbon dioxide is a major contributor.

TE begins with Lake Chad, once widely portrayed as a poster child for impending climate catastrophe. Drought, along with substantial diversion of water for irrigation, caused the lake to shrink dramatically between the 1960s and 1990s. With global temperatures rising and the Sahara supposedly advancing, the magazine notes, Lake Chad “seemed destined to disappear.”

TE reports that Lake Chad now contains more water than it has had in decades. A World Bank and International Water Management Institute study cited by the magazine found that its open-water area more than doubled after 2012, exceeding 8,300 square kilometers in 2025. Other major African water bodies, including Lakes Victoria, Malawi, Tanganyika, and Turkana, have also risen sharply.

Even more interesting is what is happening on land. TE acknowledges that satellite imagery shows substantial portions of the Sahel becoming greener as formerly parched areas revive. Increased rainfall is certainly an important contributor to the African greening described in the article.
But there is another major contributor to global greening that deserves considerably more attention: carbon dioxide.
NASA addressed this directly a decade ago in an article with the remarkably straightforward title, “Carbon Dioxide Fertilization Greening Earth, Study Finds.”

Using satellite observations from NASA’s Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Advanced Very High Resolution Radiometer, an international team of 32 researchers examined changes in leaf area between 1982 and 2015.

NASA reported that between one-quarter and one-half of Earth’s vegetated land had experienced significant greening during those 35 years. The increase in leaves on plants and trees was equivalent to adding a green area roughly twice the size of the continental United States.

According to NASA, their estimates attributed about 70 percent of the observed greening effect to carbon dioxide fertilization. Nitrogen deposition was a distant second at 9 percent, while land-use and climatic changes also contributed.
As illustrated in the infographic below, plants consume carbon dioxide through photosynthesis, greening the planet in the process.
articles.lede: Africa is getting greener and water more plentiful. Formerly parched land is supporting more vegetation and lakes are refilling.

articles.title: Un “Nor’easter” durante el Día de Acción de Gracias traerá vientos huracanados, lluvias torrenciales y niveles del agua cercanos a máximos históricos
articles.description: Se esperan graves inundaciones costeras que azotarán zonas desde los Outer Banks de Carolina del Norte hasta Long Island, Nueva York, mientras que las lluvias intensas y los fuertes vientos se extenderán mucho más allá de la costa, afectando también a regiones del interior.
paragraphs: Como si estuviera programada para coincidir con las festividades, la tormenta del noreste (nor’easter) más intensa de la temporada hasta ahora azotará la costa este de Estados Unidos desde la noche del miércoles hasta el jueves 26 de noviembre, Día de Acción de Gracias. Dos potentes sistemas de baja presión en los niveles superiores de la atmósfera se fusionarán mientras giran uno alrededor del otro. Debajo de ellos, una poderosa baja presión en superficie se intensificará rápidamente a medida que avance hacia el noreste cerca de la costa. Esta tormenta coincidirá con una superluna casi llena y un extenso corredor de vientos provenientes del océano, lo que elevará el nivel del mar hasta valores que normalmente solo se observan cada 10 a 15 años. En algunos lugares, podrían acercarse a máximos históricos.

Para la mañana del martes, ya se habían emitido avisos de inundaciones costeras en el noreste de Carolina del Norte, Virginia, Delaware y Nueva Jersey. Los fuertes vientos también podrían derribar árboles y derribar tendidos eléctricos, incluso en zonas alejadas de la costa.

Aunque no sufran inundaciones directamente, millones de personas a lo largo del densamente poblado corredor de la autopista interestatal 95 enfrentarán lluvias intensas y vientos fuertes con ráfagas mientras se reúnen para celebrar el feriado. Las precipitaciones podrían acumularse rápidamente entre 1 y 4 pulgadas (25 a 102 mm) en las zonas costeras y cercanas al litoral, desde Carolina del Norte hasta Maine. Se pronostican vientos sostenidos superiores al umbral de tormenta tropical (39 mph o 63 km/h), con ráfagas generalizadas de 50 a 60 mph (80 a 97 km/h) tierra adentro y velocidades aún mayores en la costa. Estas condiciones afectarán los Outer Banks durante la noche del miércoles y se extenderán hasta las costas de Nueva Inglaterra el jueves.

Los fuertes vientos podrían impedir que vuelen los enormes globos característicos del Desfile del Día de Acción de Gracias de Macy’s en Manhattan. De ocurrir, sería la primera vez en 55 años que los famosos globos no participarían. Las regulaciones municipales prohíben el uso de globos grandes cuando los vientos sostenidos superan las 23 mph (37 km/h) o las ráfagas superan las 34 mph (55 km/h).

Un aspecto favorable es que esta tormenta se desplazará rápidamente, avanzando desde las proximidades de los Outer Banks hacia Nueva Inglaterra durante el jueves. Otro factor importante es que no se producirá una tormenta extremadamente fría a finales de noviembre. Cualquier episodio inicial de nieve o hielo durante el jueves probablemente se limitará a las zonas más elevadas de la cordillera de los Apalaches, así como a sectores del interior de Nueva York y del norte de Nueva Inglaterra.

Entre la noche del jueves y el viernes, la parte posterior del sistema de baja presión en altura, cada vez más frío y consolidado, podría generar una franja relativamente estrecha pero intensa de nevadas desde el “Cinturón Agrícola del Maíz” (Corn Belt) hasta los Apalaches centrales. Las nevadas más abundantes probablemente se producirán en el sureste de Canadá. Para comienzos de la próxima semana, la tormenta debería ser un recuerdo lejano, ya que se pronostican temperaturas superiores a los 60 °F (16 °C) incluso en zonas tan septentrionales como Nueva Jersey.

articles.title: How COP31 fell short on easing access to finance for vulnerable nations
articles.description: An action plan proposed by Australia failed to fly after small island nations and least-developed countries decided they couldn't back it, leaving a hastily improvised committee to take discussions forward
paragraphs: Going into COP31, co-president Australia had talked up its plan to use the summit as an opportunity to make it easier for vulnerable countries to access climate finance. But during the two-week talks in Turkiye, the effort flopped when it failed to secure support from the very nations it intended to help.

An action plan and statement on improving access to finance for small island developing states (SIDS) and least-developed countries (LDCs) was presented at October’s pre-COP meeting in Fiji, and opened for governments to endorse.

articles.title: Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’?
articles.description: In this article, Carbon Brief draws together media reactions from around the world to show the diversity of responses to the COP31 outcome.
paragraphs: COP31 came to a dramatic close last weekend when a coalition of nations rejected the proposed “Antalya pact”, citing its failure to mention fossil fuels.
The tense final moments and lack of a much-anticipated “pact” have sparked extensive media coverage around the world.
Many commentators have rushed to label the COP31 outcome a “ failure ”, questioning what it means for the future of the UN climate process and a “ divided world ”.
There has been much finger-pointing, with some outlets attributing COP31’s “collapse” to “ oil-rich nations ”, while others blame Europe’s “ reluctance” to provide more climate finance.
While it is not accurate to say there was “ no agreement” at COP31, the media response demonstrates the complexity of the divergent views on display at the Antalya conference.
COP31 ended without agreement on a proposed “Antalya pact”, which had been pushed by the Turkey-Australia presidency.
The final text was rejected by at least 32 countries, including the EU, the UK and some climate-vulnerable countries, in chaotic scenes as the talks overran by two days.
An Irish Times editorial said the outcome was an “unprecedented ending of a COP without any agreement or roadmap forward”.
As veteran “COP-watchers” explained for an article on CB Connect, the summit reached agreement on many decisions, even though the presidency’s “cover decision” failed.

Referring to the rejection of the cover decision, Melbourne University climate researchers Prof Jacqueline Peel and Prof Kathryn Bowen wrote in the Conversation that “these texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process”.
articles.lede: In this article, Carbon Brief draws together media reactions from around the world to show the diversity of responses to the COP31 outcome.

NASA’s Hubble Views Ocean of Stars in Groundwork for Roman
articles.description: These Hubble observations will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations.
paragraphs: An expanse of stars gleams in a rainbow of colors in these NASA Hubble Space Telescope images of the Milky Way. The images focus on an area of sky toward the galactic bulge, a densely packed, spherical region of stars that surrounds the center of a galaxy’s disk. These Hubble observations are part of a survey that will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations as they seek to characterize the stars and search for exoplanets in this busy region of our galaxy.

Astronomers study the Milky Way’s galactic bulge because it holds nearly a quarter of the galaxy’s stellar mass, and its proximity allows them to examine the region in greater detail. Although we can see the glow from these crowded spheres of stars in other galaxies, they are too jam-packed and far away to resolve individual stars. By studying the Milky Way’s galactic bulge, researchers hope to find new planets and better understand how galaxies form, evolve, and interact over billions of years.

Hubble views the universe primarily in ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared light, while Roman collects data in near-infrared light and some visible light. Because researchers wish to compare Hubble’s observations to future Roman observations, Hubble looked at the region in wavelengths that overlap with Roman’s areas of sensitivity, the red end of the visible spectrum and near-infrared wavelengths.

Hubble’s high resolution allows its instruments to collect data on the brightness, ages, composition, and motion of stars over time. With this knowledge, astronomers can search for potential exoplanets, determine the location of black holes or dark matter, and better understand our galaxy’s environment and evolution.

A key component of Roman’s future observations is the search for exoplanets by capturing microlensing events, a type of gravitational lensing that occurs when light from a more distant object is magnified and distorted by the mass of a closer object along the line of sight. The way light from the distant star is distorted and magnified can reveal clues to the nature of the foreground star and any planets it may have. Hubble's observations will help characterize stars in the region before they undergo a lensing event. Months or years in the future, when Roman captures a microlensing event, researchers can compare Hubble data to Roman data of the event, making it easer to interpret. These microlensing events are on a much smaller scale, that of stars and planets, than larger gravitational lenses that occur around galaxies and galaxy clusters.

Over Hubble’s lifetime, it has observed our galaxy’s central bulge many times. These legacy surveys include the WFC3 Galactic Bulge Treasury Program that used Hubble’s Wide Field Camera 3 to study the brightness, precise positions, and motions of stars in this congested part of our galaxy. It also includes the Sagittarius Window Eclipsing Extrasolar Planet Search (SWEEPS) that used Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys to look at 180,000 stars in the bulge of our galaxy. These new observations come from an observing program (# 17776: S. Terry) designed to aid Roman in its search for exoplanets, black holes, neutron stars, and more. The data also adds to Hubble’s continuing legacy of high-precision observations of stars in the galactic bulge.
articles.lede: These Hubble observations will help researchers better interpret upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope observations.

articles.title: World has six consecutive days 2C above preindustrial levels for first time
articles.description: Daily global surface temperature hit record 2.24C above baseline levels on Monday and streak is forecast to continue
paragraphs: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned.

This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating.

The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days.

“This is an exceptional global temperature anomaly,” said Samantha Burgess, the strategic lead for climate at the Copernicus Climate Change Service. “We have seen record global temperatures persist for several months now. While individual days fluctuate, temperatures at this level are a striking indication of how much the climate has heated.”
There have only been two other periods when daily temperatures climbed over 2C, in November 2023 and February 2024, but they did not last as long or climb as high as this latest spell.

“Another day, another global temperature record,” said Zeke Hausfather, a climate researcher at Berkeley Earth,, adding that the previous record of 2.05C over the 1850-1900 baseline, set in 2023, has been “smashed”.
The temperature spikes are driven by long-term global heating caused by humans burning fossil fuels, and by an unusually large El Niño, which is approaching its peak.

The last El Niño on this scale was in the 1870s, when it led to a mass famine that killed 50 million people, Burgess said. Scientists expect the current El Niño to peak between now and January, though its full impact will not be felt until several months afterwards.
The extra heat in the global system is already creating feedbacks that worsen the climate crisis, such as drought and fire in the tropical rainforests of Indonesia and in the Amazon.
articles.lede: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned.

articles.title: Permitting Reform’s $199 Billion Wind and Solar Subsidy Blowout
articles.description: Our analysis concluded that BAAJA’s tax bill would range from $14 billion in Rhodium’s “high-emissions” scenario to $199 billion, based on various assumptions about wind and solar capacity expansion.
paragraphs: So anyway, I started blasting. Pow! Pow! Now, I don’t see so good, so I missed. -Frank Reynolds

As we discussed in our piece Gut Reactions to the Midterms, the recent elections greatly increase the odds that subsidies for wind and solar will be extended again, whether as part of a broader must-pass spending package signed in the next few years, as happened in 2019 and 2020, or under a future Democratic president.

One of the key factors keeping these subsidies in check over the last several years has been the lack of interregional transmission capacity, which has constrained wind development from approximately 2017 to the present. This is especially true in the western expanses of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) region.

However, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), a permitting reform bill that passed the U.S. Senate on Thursday night by a vote of 62-33 and now heads to the House, would lift this bottleneck by making it easier to build new transmission lines and shifting the cost of building them onto consumers like you.

In this edition of Energy Bad Boys, we discuss how this bill changes the transmission permitting process and total up the billions of dollars in additional wind and solar subsidies that are likely to stem from BAAJA.

“BAAJA would expedite the transmission buildout by greatly expanding federal “backstop” siting authority, deeming any transmission line selected in a regional or interregional plan, including plans built to serve state renewable mandates, to meet the federal permit criteria. This means a state could reject an interstate transmission line, but FERC must approve it anyway simply because a regional planner put it on the map and it meets several loosely defined criteria.

It would also foist more of the cost of that transmission onto ratepayers, rather than the wind and solar developers who need it in the first place, by allocating costs to anyone deemed to “benefit” from a line. However, the bill broadly defines the term “benefit,” and FERC has previously stretched that term to include progress toward state public-policy goals.

In other words, residents in states without renewable energy mandates could end up being forced to pay for the transmission lines primarily needed to help states with aggressive wind and solar mandates, like Michigan, Minnesota, and Illinois, meet their own policy goals.

With the hurdles of backstop authority and cost allocation out of the way, which can add years to the permitting process, BAAJA would greatly expand the projected wind and solar capacity on the books.
We compiled several studies that measure the impact of permitting reform on power capacity buildout in the U.S.
articles.lede: Our analysis concluded that BAAJA’s tax bill would range from $14 billion in Rhodium’s “high-emissions” scenario to $199 billion, based on various assumptions about wind and solar capacity expansion.

Spain has been hit hard by the climate crisis. Why are politicians saying so little about it before the election?
articles.description: Wildfires and floods can do little to move climate change up voters’ list of priorities, experts say
paragraphs: B eneath the blackened branches of a pine tree that rises high above a landscape of scorched hillsides and the odd charred and ruined house, two older men address the obvious. Four months after one of the summer’s many wildfires threatened to devour the hamlet of El Morro, an hour west of Madrid, local people are still counting the cost and awaiting compensation.

“Look at that house,” said Esteban Pérez, pointing to one of the properties that did not make it through July’s flames. “Everything inside is scorched, completely destroyed. You can still see the windows, but they’re gutted. The entire structure of the house next to mine had to be torn down, too. And they’ve given the owner nothing so far.”

And yet, for all the abundant recent evidence of the effects of the climate crisis around Spain’s capital and in the eastern region of Valencia, which is still recovering from the deadly floods that killed more than 230 people two years ago, there has been little mention of the issue as the country prepares for this week’s snap general election.
Pérez is not surprised that the politicians are keener to focus on housing and immigration than on Spain’s immense vulnerability to climatic disasters and the attendant costs.
“The thing is, they only talk about whatever interests them during the campaign,” he said. “If something doesn’t interest them, they don’t talk about it.”

Four hundred kilometres to the east in the Valencian municipality of Benetússer, Rut Moyano, a member of the local emergency and reconstruction committee, has been stunned by the lack of focus on the climate crisis.

“It’s not just the floods we have experienced, there are also the forest fires; the temperatures the Mediterranean is reaching; the fact that we spend our summers in a state of permanent heatwave, and the droughts,” she said.

“Everything is changing because of these factors, but it’s as if there’s an attempt – I don’t know if it’s an intentional silencing – but certainly a failure to give the issue the importance it truly deserves.”
Despite the lack of stump speeches and calls to action, climate policies do feature in this year’s manifestos.

Low-interest loans help Vermont towns recover from devastating floods
articles.description: The Vermont Bond Bank launched a climate recovery fund to help municipalities cover infrastructure repairs after extreme weather.
paragraphs: In July, 2023, heavy rain unleashed catastrophic flooding across much of Vermont. Then, a year later to the day, it happened again.

For hard-hit cities and towns, the expense of clearing debris and repairing roads and other infrastructure was staggering. And in some small municipalities, the cost far exceeded their entire annual budget.
Gaughan: “And so caused an issue where they, in select cases, were pushing up against the amounts that their banking relationships would lend to them.”
The state created the bond bank in 1970 to help cities and towns access low-interest financing for infrastructure.
In response to the flooding, the bond bank launched a municipal climate recovery fund that offers low-interest loans to help cities and towns rebuild.
Gaughan says the fund has helped municipalities across Vermont cover critical costs while they wait for FEMA reimbursements.
This fall, Indiana’s bond bank launched a similar program after floods there. And other bond banks across the U.S. could follow suit as climate change fuels more extreme weather.

articles.description: A state with one of the highest energy burdens in the nation considers ways to rein in utility spending.
paragraphs: That’s how Seth Berry describes rising electricity prices in Maine. As executive director of Our Power, a coalition focused on clean energy and utility regulation, Berry talks with people all over the state who are no longer able to afford their power bills.

Combined with recent price increases for heating fuel and gasoline, he said electricity bills could create “a world of hurt” for many Maine households this winter. “People are really at their wits’ end, and I expect to see a whole lot of folks cold this winter, desperately cold in their homes,” Berry said.

Maine has one of the highest energy burdens in the country, due in part to the cost of downed power lines and other repairs after severe storms. The state’s biggest power company is currently requesting another rate increase, and Maine is now reckoning with the balance between needed grid repairs and affordable power bills.

Electricity prices in Maine increased 64 percent between 2019 and 2025, compared to an average 38 percent increase nationwide, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Only Washington, D.C., and California had larger increases.

The state also has one of the highest average household energy burdens in the nation. A 2024 report to Maine’s Electric Ratepayer Advisory Council found that low-income households spend about 8 percent of their income on electricity and an additional 6 percent on other sources like propane and heating oil. Anything above 6 percent is considered a high energy burden by the U.S. Department of Energy.

Maine’s rural, heavily forested character means utility companies require more miles of power lines to reach their most remote customers, and these lines are more likely to be hit by tree branches, the most common cause of outages.

articles.title: Eurofreezin’
articles.description: The ultimate irony: The country that was under Marxist domination for almost a half-century has its energy house in order, to the extent it could be.
paragraphs: There is so much trashing of any idea that may run counter to a message being pushed on people that AI has become an invaluable tool for me to try to stay objective. So, in evaluating what is going on in Europe, I went to the AI to ask what contribution does energy policy have in this matter to another winter — this one looking colder than last winter, when many places saw their energy storage levels fall dangerously low.
Policies play a meaningful structural role and have shaped the environment in which these market and shock factors play out:

In short, the rigid post-2022 storage mandates and the deliberate shift away from Russian supplies made Europe more dependent on expensive, globally competitive LNG and on policy-driven storage floors. When market conditions and the Hormuz disruption made high commercial fills uneconomic, the system responded with target flexibility and ad-hoc interventions rather than full market-driven refills. Officials maintain preparedness is adequate for a normal winter, but the thinner buffers and higher costs are direct consequences of both the external shock and the policy framework that reduced cheaper pipeline options while requiring high storage.

The proximate cause of the 2026 shortfall is the combination of negative price signals and the Middle East LNG disruption; Europe’s energy policies are a significant enabling and amplifying structural contributor.

Now I wrote about this last year. Europe is already turning cold, as we warned it would once the heavy rains started in Western Europe. A wet November and early December in Europe signals a cold December. It means storms are cutting east under a developing blocking upper ridge, not lifting northeast. No better example than 2009, which was an El Niño year.
We have turned quite wet in Western Europe, and here we go. The Euro weeklies look like this:

The ensembles (first one) are a blend of many members. However, the weather will only go to one solution. So the control shows us where this could go and what it’s likely to trend toward. The first one is crucial; the second option would be a disaster, since it would take a warm rest of the winter to keep storage from falling to levels that could mean rationing.
There are countries like Poland and Sweden that, for some reason, are filled almost to capacity.
What impact could this have? Obviously less in Poland, but let’s take the most egregious case: the UK.

The UK is designed for rapid response to cold snaps. An interesting idea, given the chaotic world situation. But what if it went to the cold levels of 2009-10? (Heck, I am not even going to go to the El Niño year of 1986-87, which was colder.)
articles.lede: The ultimate irony: The country that was under Marxist domination for almost a half-century has its energy house in order, to the extent it could be.

articles.description: State regulators are pressing the Air Force to meet cleanup deadlines for an ongoing jet fuel leak. A separate fight over a golf course renovation is testing the state’s regulatory reach.
paragraphs: Recent testing at Joint Base Andrews found a thick layer of jet fuel beneath the airfield, eight months after a spill was detected near Piscataway Creek. But the Air Force and Maryland environmental regulators remain at odds over basic facts of the spill, such as how much fuel was leaked and whether the base skipped its reporting obligations, while the leak’s source has yet to be found.

At the same time, they are locked in a separate dispute over a golf course renovation, which the base says is beyond the reach of the state’s regulatory authority due to an exemption from President Donald Trump.

Between Nov. 9 and 13, the Air Force conducted pressure testing and drilled several soil borings along the section of pipeline where the leak was suspected. Maryland inspectors were also on site watching. One boring, along a pipe known as Lateral Row 7, found a layer of fuel 3.32-feet-thick, the Air Force said.

In separate statements, both sides said the finding significantly narrowed the search. But neither can yet determine where exactly the pipe broke. The Air Force said that will require digging the line up or inspecting it directly.

articles.title: New Paper Challenges Cruelty Exemptions for Food-Producing Animals
articles.description: One lawyer makes a case that could open pathways for prosecuting cruelty that’s been legally treated as accepted practice.
paragraphs: Clipping off chickens’ sensitive beaks without anesthesia. Cramming sows in crates so small they can’t turn around. Castrating or dehorning livestock without painkillers. Slamming piglets on the ground to kill them—a practice known in the industry as “thumping.”

These are all considered standard, common or accepted practice in U.S. animal agriculture and are exempt from state animal cruelty laws. Even in a country that overwhelmingly says it wants animals treated well—not just the 150 million or so kept as pets, but the 10 billion raised for food—this is the status quo.

The vast majority of the animals that are consumed or generate animal products in the United States are raised in intensive confinement, out of public view. Animal cruelty laws largely don’t apply to them mostly because of the immense power of the American farm lobby, which has convinced lawmakers that the industry itself can decide what is standard practice and therefore legal.
But a new paper argues that these exemptions for food-producing animals—which have been widely accepted as the norm for decades, even by animal advocacy groups—aren’t legally ironclad after all.

COP31 collides with Stop Fossil Fuel movement
articles.description: Our civilization is presently run on fossil fuels and there is no feasible alternative. Any serious attempt to reduce fossil fuel use is bound to be bad.
paragraphs: COP31 systematically ignored the growing green movement focused on the (impossible) ending of fossil fuel use and it bit them hard. This movement threatens to compete with the COP process by pulling action away. The COP also gave a hard push in that destabilizing direction. So the movement shut the COP down.

Three months ago I pointed out two potentially destabilizing activities that are core features of the movement. The movement even has an easy acronym: TAFF which stands for Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels.

The first activity is the development of a model international treaty to end fossil fuel use. The COP is itself based on a 1992 treaty which many green activists say is going nowhere. A new treaty might well compete with the COP treaty for attention and resources, even to the point of putting COPs out of business.

This startup TAFF treaty activity was officially ignored at COP31. Negotiations began with an 18 page, 147 item listing of potential considerations and findings. The word “treaty” did not appear once in that lengthy issue list. The COP could have tried to co-opt the treaty movement but it conspicuously failed to do so.

The second activity is promoting the country by country development of national “roadmaps” or plans for phasing out the use of fossil fuels. These roadmaps (to impossibility) are an obvious big step toward ratifying a treaty with the same (impossible) end. That it cannot possibly be done is irrelevant to the present politics.
The big issue list used the term roadmap many times but never to refer to this growing green movement. It was decisively ignored.
Then the COP opened the TAFF floodgates. While the first long draft of issues at least included something about reducing fossil fuel use the second draft dropped the term “fossil fuel” altogether.
Many COP delegates were TAFF proponents and they were outraged. TAFF quickly became the defining issue, driving the COP into protracted overtime then collapse. The collision was complete.

The TAFF issue is extreme. Opponents to TAFF say the COP is about emission reduction not fuel use. In fact the net zero doctrine allows for some fossil fuel emissions as long as these are offset. That is what “net” means.

Nor are major fossil fuel exporting countries willing to commit to abandoning that income. In fact Australia, which exports about a third of global coal by value, was in charge of COP31 negotiations. Russia won’t give up on gas nor Saudi Arabia on oil and so on. These are the realists.

El Niño Giveth and Taketh Away. NOAA Credits a Natural Cycle for a Record Pacific Season and a One-Hurricane Atlantic
articles.description: NOAA's wrap-up credits El Niño, a natural phenomenon, for a record Pacific ACE and a one-hurricane Atlantic. The record is energy, not storm count.
paragraphs: NOAA published its 2026 hurricane season wrap-up today under the headline “El Nino fueled record number of Pacific storms but calmed Atlantic.” The Atlantic produced 10 named storms and one hurricane. The eastern and central Pacific, by NOAA’s count, had their most active season on record.

The 2026 hurricane season, which officially ends on November 30, will be remembered as a year of contrasts between the Atlantic and Pacific, a classic indication of a hurricane season influenced by a very strong El Nino. Below normal activity across the Atlantic basin was offset by above-average activity in the Pacific, including two disasters in Hawaii.

“NOAA’s unparalleled forecasting skill and scientific expertise provided the early warnings needed to protect lives and property this hurricane season,” said Neil Jacobs, Ph.D., NOAA administrator. “This included accurately predicting this year’s very strong El Nino months in advance, which gave us the critical insight we needed to accurately forecast this season.”

NOAA did get the direction right in both oceans. The May 21 Atlantic outlook gave 8–14 named storms, 3–6 hurricanes, 1–3 major hurricanes and ACE of 45–115% of the median. The August 6 update trimmed that to 7–13, 2–6, 0–2 and 30–90%. The season delivered 10 named storms, one hurricane and one major hurricane, and NHC’s season table puts Atlantic ACE at 20.2, 83% below the 1991–2020 normal. That is roughly a fifth of the 1951–2020 median NOAA’s ranges are built on, under the floor of both outlooks, and one hurricane missed the bottom of both hurricane ranges too. The August outlook said strong El Niño seasons had historically produced 2–4 hurricanes and ACE of 33–89% of the median, so 2026 came in under that as well. “Accurately” is a generous word for it, though nobody on the Gulf Coast will complain about a forecast that missed in that direction.

One hurricane is the fewest in the Atlantic since 1925 in NOAA’s HURDAT2 database, a point Florida Atlantic University also made on November 16. NOAA says Isaias’s October 7 formation was the latest for a season’s first hurricane since the satellite era began in 1966. Readers here watched it happen; Chris Martz noted on September 21 that the Atlantic had reached that date without a hurricane for the first time since 1914.
In the Atlantic panel most of the orange bars sit near the bottom, with 2023 the exception. This year is the second lowest since 1971, behind 1983.
On the Pacific, the headline says a record number of storms, and the body of the release says something else:

The combined central and eastern Pacific basin had its most active hurricane season on record. NOAA measures a season’s overall tropical activity by its Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE), which refers to the combined intensity and duration of tropical storms and hurricanes occurring during the season. In total, the Pacific basin had an ACE of 359.5, surpassing the old record of 318 in 2018.

That record holds up. NHC’s eastern Pacific table (247.5) plus CPHC’s central Pacific table (112.0) gives NOAA’s 359.5, and summing the HURDAT2 best tracks east of the dateline for 2018 gives 318.1, the figure NOAA cites. ACE squares the wind speed every six hours, so a handful of long-lived Category 4 and 5 storms do most of the work. Polo alone logged 50.2 units in the eastern Pacific, more than twice the Atlantic’s whole season. The numbers are preliminary until NHC finishes its post-season reports.
articles.lede: NOAA's wrap-up credits El Niño, a natural phenomenon, for a record Pacific ACE and a one-hurricane Atlantic. The record is energy, not storm count.

articles.title: Why are people captivated by this photo of a crowded Chris Bowen scowling? Is it the negative space?
articles.description: Australia’s climate change minister was president of negotiations at Cop31 in Turkey when it all went a bit sideways
paragraphs: Blake, I was at the back of the huge plenary hall in Antalya on Sunday at the end of the UN climate summit that overran by two days. For about 20 minutes, you could see from the panic on the stage that it wasn’t going well.

I only had an old iPhone, was a long way back, and remember thinking ‘I’d love a long lens to see the expression on their faces’. Then came this incredible picture of Chris Bowen looking like all his Christmases had come at once and every present was a jumper he hates. Why can’t I stop looking at it?
It’s tragedy and resignation. On reflection my Christmas jumper analogy probably wasn’t the best. It’s planet-defining stuff all of this. Sorry, what? Negative space?
That’s the area above his head with nothing in it. It’s shaped like a V and it’s drawing your eyes down to this amazing expression that I’ve actually seen Bowen make before. He does it occasionally.

Yes and no. Not many other photographers have that frame. If the photographer, Murad Sezer, had been a few metres to one side it would have been really different. But he made choices about where to be and what to focus on. Technically, though, it’s not perfect. The lady on the far left …
Well she’s cropped in half. That’s not perfect. And there’s a guy with the top of his head chopped off. This is starting to sound bad.

Not really. Murad wasn’t lucky. He would have been looking at body language and the people behind Bowen and then shooting in bursts. I’ve seen the other frames and there’s only a few that catch that expression. We can forgive the cropping because it perfectly tells the story of the moment and what Bowen must have been thinking. That it’s all gone to shit and can this all be over? Well, yes. But the people above him look like they’re still trying to work things out, actually. So there’s intrigue. Was everything lost at that point? Maybe. The picture was taken before the plenary had started properly. I remember thinking, this looks as though the Australians know they don’t have consensus.

Those of us in the room only knew for sure they hadn’t reached consensus once the meeting got going and countries started interjecting. It was high drama. Consensus is not quite the same as unanimity, but it’s close.

I thought you were explaining this to me? They’re political and department staff from Australia. Negotiators, department experts and there’s a senior media advisor in there – she’s second from the right. All exhausted after two weeks and days of all-night negotiations. With so much on the line, I don’t think I would have fancied being any of them.
articles.lede: Blake, I was at the back of the huge plenary hall in Antalya on Sunday at the end of the UN climate summit that overran by two days. For about 20 minutes, you could see from the panic on the stage that it wasn’t going well.

paragraphs: The first thing renowned climatologist Daniel Swain did during his virtual office hours on Monday was set the record straight about California’s upcoming flood risk. This week, water levels along the state’s coast, bays and estuaries will be as high, if not higher, than they’ve ever been, he said.

“But this will not, I repeat, will not be because of extreme rainfall,” said Swain, a University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources weather and climate scientist who regularly hosts briefings to explain global warming’s effects on natural hazards.

Some news reports and government officials were blaming predicted record-breaking coastal flooding on extreme storms. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie, for example, said the city would see rainfall “that this city had never seen before.” Others warned people living inland to prepare for severe flooding.
“None of that is accurate,” Swain said. “This is not being really driven by rain or a storm at all.”

articles.title: Brother, Can You Spare a Basis Point? PNAS Paper Blames Storms for a Fifth of Tropical Countries’ Debt
articles.description: When the authors went looking for a debt effect from warming, they didn't find one.
paragraphs: On November 17, PNAS published “ The debt burden of tropical cyclones and climate change” by June Choi, Renzhi Jing, Christopher Callahan, Marshall Burke and Noah Diffenbaugh, all of Stanford when the work was done. Stanford’s press office followed on November 23 with “ Cyclones and heat have added billions to global debt ,” the day after COP31 in Antalya, which the release itself notes ended without advancing on key climate finance targets.

We provide evidence that the cost and availability of capital for many countries have already been shaped by both historical exposure to naturally-occurring tropical cyclones (TCs) and anthropogenic warming. Our empirical estimates suggest that, on average across TC-exposed countries, 20% of debt-to-GDP ratios are attributable to TCs from 1980 to 2019. Across all countries, GDP levels are on average 12% lower due to the combined impacts of baseline naturally-occurring TCs and anthropogenic warming. In a separate correlational machine-learning analysis, we estimate that these macroeconomic impacts are associated with an increased likelihood of hotter countries receiving credit ratings below investment grade (≤ BBB–), as well as persistent credit risk premiums of at least 1 basis point in 64 countries and 5 basis points in highly exposed countries.

“Naturally-occurring” shows up twice in four sentences, and the authors mean it. The 20 per cent is debt blamed on hurricanes and typhoons as they have always come ashore. When the authors went looking for a debt effect from warming, they didn’t find one:
We do not detect a clear impact of temperature on the debt ratio separate from TCs, as coefficients are highly sensitive to the inclusion of different samples and time trends (SI Appendix, Fig. S6).

Stanford’s release puts it more plainly: “ Warming alone showed no clear effect on debt ratios, however.” Diffenbaugh, a senior author, says in the same release that the study “shines a new light on the role of tropical cyclones in shaping the historical debt burden of small island states, irrespective of climate change.” So the climate change in the title rests on the GDP side of the paper and on one sensitivity test, buried in the Results:

In an alternate hypothetical scenario, we conduct a sensitivity test assuming all TCs had 10% less intense wind speeds during 1980–2019, 10% being a global upper bound estimate on the influence of global warming on TC intensity (59–61). In this scenario, debt ratio impacts would have decreased by 17 to 40% (P25–P75).

Take the authors’ own upper bound, apply it to every storm for forty years, and climate change’s share of the debt comes to roughly 3 to 8 per cent of debt ratios in exposed countries, by my arithmetic. That assumes the storms really did get 10 per cent stronger. The IPCC’s Sixth Assessment Report says of the storm record:

There is low confidence in most reported long-term (multi-decadal to centennial) trends in TC frequency- or intensity-based metrics due to changes in the technology used to collect the best-track data.
articles.lede: When the authors went looking for a debt effect from warming, they didn't find one.

Climate scientists urge US lawmakers to vote no on sweeping permitting bill
articles.description: Open letter warns Baaja, intended to expedite energy and infrastructure projects, will cause irreversible climate harm
paragraphs: A group of more than 120 climate scientists have urged US lawmakers to not pass contentious legislation to speed up the building of energy projects, datacenters and other infrastructure, amid a growing backlash to the sweeping permitting bill.

In an open letter to members of the House of Representatives, the collection of Earth and social sciences researchers expressed “deep concern” that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (or Baaja) weakens environmental laws, locks in new fossil fuel projects without recourse and delivers only minor cuts to planet-heating emissions.
“We understand the need for trade-offs and compromise when passing bipartisan legislation,” they wrote. “But as scientists we feel strongly that the costs of this bill to the climate are too high.”

Last week, the US Senate rapidly passed Baaja, a bill co-written by two Democratic and two Republican senators but one that has bitterly divided Democrats and environmentalists. The House is set to vote on the bill next week, where it will be signed by Donald Trump into law if passed.

Michael Mann, a climate scientist who helped arrange the open letter, said that he did so because Baaja is a “deeply problematic bill” that is “backed by a veritable who’s who of bad fossil fuel and dark money actors”.

Mann said that Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, should “scrap Baaja, which in the end only takes us further down the dangerous fossil fuel pathway, and put a sensible, popular datacenter bill on Trump’s desk and force him to veto it. And force Republicans to defend sustaining that veto.”

Timmons Roberts, a Brown University academic and letter co-signatory, said the bill is “very worrisome, it has felt very rushed and there is grave potential for damage that can’t be done any time soon”.

“We are in a broken system, and it’s hard to build anything, but there has to be a better way to do this,” Roberts added. “In some ways it feels like we are being held hostage. If you want more renewables you have to also see the lock-in of fossil fuels and the devastating gutting of core legislation that has allowed the US to improve its natural environment.”

Mann said that Sheldon Whitehouse, the Democratic senator and longtime champion of climate action who has co-sponsored Baaja, has “long been one of my heroes, and nothing pains me to find him not only in support of the bill but in fact one of its principal backers”.

articles.description: Coastal flooding is expected to slam areas from the Outer Banks of North Carolina to Long Island, New York, and heavy rains and high winds will extend well inland.
paragraphs: As if on holiday cue, the season’s biggest nor’easter thus far will rake the U.S. East Coast from Wednesday night into Thursday, November 26, Thanksgiving Day. Two strong upper-level areas of low pressure will consolidate as they pivot around each other. Beneath these, a powerful surface low will intensify as it zips northeast near the coast. This storm will team up with a nearly full “ supermoon” and a long fetch of onshore wind to push coastal water to levels observed only once every 10-15 years, perhaps approaching all-time high-water marks in some spots. Coastal flood watches were already in place Tuesday morning along the coasts of northeast North Carolina, Virginia, Delaware, and New Jersey, and trees and power lines could be felled by high winds even well inland.

Even if they’re not dealing with flooding themselves, millions of folks along the populous Interstate 95 corridor will face drenching rains and fierce, gusty winds as they gather for the holiday. Rainfall could quickly total anywhere from one to four inches along and near the coast from North Carolina to Maine. Sustained winds above tropical-storm force (39 mph), with widespread gusts of 50-60 mph inland and even higher values along the coast, are predicted to sweep across the Outer Banks on Wednesday night and from Chesapeake Bay to coastal New England during the day on Thursday.

The high winds may end up grounding the huge balloons synonymous with the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in Manhattan; if so, it will be the first absence of the famed balloons in 55 years. (City regulations prohibit large balloons if winds are sustained above 23 mph or gusting above 34 mph.)

One saving grace is that this storm will be a fast mover, racing from near the Outer Banks to New England through the day on Thursday. Another key aspect: This won’t be a brutally cold storm for late November. Any initial snow and ice on Thursday will likely be limited to the highest terrain of the Appalachians, as well as parts of interior New York and northern New England.

Late Thursday and Friday, the back side of the cold, consolidating upper low may generate a small but potent corridor of tail-end snow across the Corn Belt and into the central Appalachians, with the heaviest snows likely to develop over southeast Canada. By early next week, the storm should be a distant memory, as readings above 60°F are predicted to make their way as far north as New Jersey.

paragraphs: Ed. Note: This open letter from Judith Curry to the next generation of her profession, inspired by the email release dubbed Climategate, remains important with the 17th anniversary of IPCC science scandal (2009). It was Michael “Climategate” Mann who infamously stated: “ I gave up on Judith Curry a while ago. I don’t know what she thinks she’s doing, but it’s not helping the cause.”

“What has been noticeably absent so far in the ClimateGate discussion is a public reaffirmation by climate researchers of our basic research values: the rigors of the scientific method (including reproducibility), research integrity and ethics, open minds, and critical thinking. Under no circumstances should we ever sacrifice any of these values; the CRU emails, however, appear to violate them.” – Judith Curry (below)

Judith Curry recounted the “crazy days of Thanksgiving 2009 when I spent all weekend writing my ‘Open Letter’” in the wake of Climategate. At the time, Curry’s letter was reproduced by Andrew Revkin at Dot Earth at the time under the title, “ A Climate Scientist Who Engages Skeptics” (November 27, 2009).

Based upon feedback that I’ve received from graduate students at Georgia Tech, I suspect that you are confused, troubled, or worried by what you have been reading about ClimateGate After spending considerable time reading the hacked emails and other posts in the blogosphere, I wrote an essay that calls for greater transparency in climate data and other methods used in climate research. The essay is posted over at climateaudit.org.

What has been noticeably absent so far in the ClimateGate discussion is a public reaffirmation by climate researchers of our basic research values: the rigors of the scientific method (including reproducibility), research integrity and ethics, open minds, and critical thinking. Under no circumstances should we ever sacrifice any of these values; the CRU emails, however, appear to violate them.

My motivation for communicating on this issue in the blogosphere comes from emails that I received from Georgia Tech graduate students and alums. As a result of my post on climateaudit, I started receiving emails from graduate students from other universities. I post the content of one of the emails here, without reference to the student’s name or institution:

I am a young climate researcher (just received my master’s degree from xxx University) and have been very troubled by the emails that were released from CRU. I just want to applaud and support your response on climatesudit.org (95% of it). Your statement represents exactly how I have felt as I slowly enter this community. The content of some of the emails literally made me stop and wonder if I should continue with my PhD applications for fall 2010, in this science.

I was so troubled by how our fellow scientists within the climate community have been dealing with opposing voices (on both sides). I hope we can all learn from this and truly feel that we are going to need voices like yours to fix these problems in the coming months and years.

articles.description: Large-scale boats were caught violating fishing rules 66 percent of the time, while small boats struggle to survive.
paragraphs: Along England’s southern coast lies a fishing community whose existence can be traced back almost a millennium. From its shingled shore, Hastings once housed the largest beach-launched fleet in Europe. But when retired fisherman Jerry Percy visited a few weeks ago, he could count the operational boats on his fingers.

“If you take the argument to the end game, then you’ll have nothing but a picture-postcard fleet bobbing about in little pretty harbors and bugger-all else,” said Percy, describing a “spiral of decline” across the U.K.’s small-boat fleet.

This hollowing out of coastal livelihoods is part of a “rigged system,” according to a new report by Oceana UK. Unequal government subsidies, outdated quota systems and catch limits that routinely ignore science have concentrated wealth in large corporate fleets at the expense of coastal communities and the marine ecosystems they rely on.

“The non-compliance, the discards, the very poor transparency and the quota inequality is all really adding up,” said Izzy Ross, Oceana UK’s habitats and fisheries campaign manager. “It’s not a fair playing field for those who want to do things right and want to do things more sustainably.”

Summer heat deaths in 2026 reached record high of 5,258 in England
articles.description: Figure for May to September is far higher than previous peak of 2,985 since records began a decade ago
paragraphs: More than 5,200 deaths in England in 2026 were linked to summer heat, the highest provisional annual total since records began a decade ago, according to the UK Health Security Agency.
The government agency said 5,258 deaths were associated with extreme heat between May and September 2026.
The figure is substantially higher than the previous record of 2,985, recorded in 2022, and follows totals of 2,295 in 2023, 1,311 in 2024 and 1,504 last year.

This year’s summer was the hottest on record, bringing record-breaking temperatures and prolonged dry weather. Temperatures reached 38C (100.4F) in Norfolk in June, while a peak of 38.2C was recorded in Gloucestershire in August. England also experienced its driest July on record, with just 7mm of rain.

The greatest number of deaths was during the heatwave between 21 and 28 June, when an estimated 2,401 people died. More than 3,000 heat-associated deaths were recorded across the first two episodes of the season, in May and June.

The agency said the summer had seven “heat episodes” lasting a total of 41 days, the highest number of episodes and heat-episode days since monitoring began in 2016. The June heatwave triggered only the second red heat-health alert ever issued in England.

Dr Ross Thompson, UKHSA’s principal environmental health scientist, said: “Climate change is already affecting people’s health in England, and as the climate continues to warm we can expect periods of extreme heat to become longer, more frequent and more intense.”

“That is why it is vital that individuals, communities, health and care services and local organisations are prepared, not just during a heatwave but in the longer term. The decisions we make now will shape the health impacts people experience in the decades ahead.”

UKHSA said heat early in the summer could be particularly dangerous because people and public services may not yet be prepared. It said heat-health measures should be in place from the start of summer, rather than focused only on the hottest weeks.

articles.description: At COP31, Indigenous representatives warned that growing demand for lithium and uranium is threatening their lands, water, and rights.
paragraphs: ANTALYA, TURKEY – As representatives of the world’s countries gathered in Antalya, Turkey, to discuss how to accelerate the transition to climate-friendly electric technologies, Indigenous people spoke out against mining on their territories for the raw materials that the tech requires.

“Why can protecting our territories wait, but exploitation cannot? What is really urgent? What is really critical?” asked Djalma Ramalho, a member of the Aranã Caboclo community, a territory in the Jequitinhonha Valley of Brazil.

Ramalho raised this question to the audience gathered at the Indigenous peoples’ pavilion for a panel on mineral extraction. The panel set the tone for Indigenous people’s demands during negotiations at the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change Conference of the Parties, also known as COP31.

Nearly 200 countries attended the recent two-week annual conference to debate an international agreement to limit climate change. Negotiations focused on the goal of rapidly increasing the share of the world’s energy needs that are met with electricity, which can be produced with climate-friendly solar, wind, and nuclear power. The talks broke down over the weekend when major oil-producing nations blocked language about phasing out fossil fuels, which cause climate change.

The push for electrification is accelerating demand for raw materials like lithium, which is used in the batteries that power electric vehicles and provide back-up power for solar panels. Production of uranium, which fuels nuclear power plants, is also rising.

That has big implications for Indigenous people: Fifty-four percent of mining projects for the minerals critical to an energy transition are located on or near Indigenous peoples’ land, according to a 2022 study. According to the World Nuclear Association, the largest-producing uranium mines are in Canada, Namibia, Kazakhstan, and Australia. Over a quarter (29%) of the uranium stemming from these mines is on recognized Indigenous land.

As demand for these materials grows, Indigenous representatives are pushing countries to write their rights into the Just Transition Mechanism, a framework agreed upon in 2025 to coordinate international cooperation, technical assistance, capacity-building, and knowledge-sharing.
Ramalho’s community in the Jequitinhonha Valley has seen firsthand the impacts of lithium extraction. Mines have contaminated waterways and exacerbated water scarcity in an already arid region.

“Our relationship with the water needs to be respected,” Ramalho said in a video produced for COP31. “This is a relationship that goes far beyond the physical. We believe the Jequitinhonha River is a reclining ancestor. Where does my ancestor go when you pollute my river? Where does my ancestor go when you kill my river? When the river has rights, life has a future.”
“They are literally destroying our territory,” Ramalho added. “Whatever the promises of clean energy development, my territory cannot be treated as a sacrifice zone for the world.”
articles.lede: At COP31, Indigenous representatives warned that growing demand for lithium and uranium is threatening their lands, water, and rights.

Gramlich: “The big transmission lines that you see when you drive along the highway are what a lot of the large wind, solar, and battery storage developers are trying to connect to, and they connect specifically to substations.”

That’s Rob Gramlich of the consulting firm Grid Strategies. He says before utilities and grid operators greenlight a project, they have to assess whether the grid can handle the added electricity in that location or whether it will require upgrades.
It’s a slow, expensive process with a long backlog. But if passed, a new federal bill would require regulators to shorten it.

And government agencies and grid operators are working to streamline the process – for example, by studying clusters of projects at once, or prioritizing projects in areas with lots of transmission capacity to get them online more quickly.
Gramlich: “The regulations are difficult, the politics are difficult, but we can overcome those things.”

El Nino To Kill Half a Million!!
articles.description: Higher temperatures linked to El Nino will very likely save lives overall.
paragraphs: It was once a proud, serious-minded newspaper, but under Axel Springer the Telegraph is rapidly turning into a laughingstock.
Scientists on Tuesday said that El Niño – predicted to be the most intense on record – should be classified as a global health emergency which could kill hundreds of thousands.

“The 2026-27 El Niño is going to cause pandemic-scale mortality,” said Dr Colin Carlson, an assistant professor of epidemiology at Yale University, warning it would be deadlier than the 2009 swine flu pandemic, which killed roughly 284,000 people.

He urged the World Health Organisation to classify the “discrete and deadly event” as a public health emergency of international concern, on par with the Ebola epidemic in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the circulation of polio.

“An early analysis suggests that nearly half a million deaths will result from extreme heat alone, to say nothing of epidemics of dengue fever, cholera, and other infectious diseases that could also occur in tandem,” Dr Carlson said, in an article in Think Global Health with Prof Christopher Callahan, a climate scientist at Indiana University.

Needless to say, none of these frankly absurd claims are based on real world data; instead, they are worked out from computer models, programmed to assume that death rates increase as temperatures do.

That real world data shows no spikes at all in mortality rates during El Nino years, such as 1998 and 2016. The spike during the pandemic is abundantly clear, a fact which itself makes the Telegraph’s claims of “pandemic-scale mortality” ludicrous.
There was, interestingly, one other, smaller spike in 1994. Chat GPT informs me this was caused by the Rwandan Genocide, during which an estimated 800,000 lost their lives.

A Lancet study in 2021 estimated that there were on average 489,075 heat-related deaths around the world each year between 2000 and 2019, but nearly 4.6 million cold-related ones. In other words, nine times as many cold-related deaths.
You can argue about the numbers, but several other studies support the basic premise that deaths from cold far outweigh those from heat.
articles.lede: Higher temperatures linked to El Nino will very likely save lives overall.

paragraphs: Montana’s snow-capped mountains, vast forests and open valleys have long attracted people seeking a life close to nature. But that lifestyle is becoming increasingly difficult to afford, or even attain, as the state’s growing wildfire risk spikes homeowners insurance premiums and leaves some home buyers unable to purchase coverage at all.

As wildfire seasons grow longer and more destructive across the American West, insurers are fundamentally changing how they evaluate risk, said James Brown, Montana’s elected state auditor, who also serves as the state’s commissioner of securities and insurance. About 70 percent of the acreage burned by wildfires in Montana since 1888 has burned since 2000, according to the state Legislature. And nearly two-thirds of Montana homes are located within the Wildland-Urban Interface, or WUI, where residential development meets fire-prone forests and grasslands, leaving them vulnerable to wildfires.

“We’re receiving more complaints from homeowners about wildfire insurance than almost any other issue,” said Brown in an interview with Inside Climate News. “People are finding that either their premiums have increased significantly or their policies are not being renewed because companies are reassessing wildfire risk.”

UCLA study masks energy industry’s environmental gains
articles.description: Studies masking as advocacy may drive clicks, but they don’t drive progress.
paragraphs: A byproduct of living in the Information Age is how easily data spreads without context. A recent UCLA analysis identifying several prominent American energy companies as major methane emitters is a case in point.

The report, released as part of its “STOP methane” project, relied on satellite observations to track methane emissions across three American oil and gas basins, which the authors selected because they “export the most LNG to Europe.” It attempts to link the observable methane emissions from these basins to specific sites and companies operating in those regions.

The authors acknowledge that publicly available data could confidently match fewer than one-third of the identified methane sources to potentially responsible owners. They also concede that even those matches are susceptible to inaccuracies.

These substantial gaps leave UCLA’s report short of a full picture and warrant caution in interpreting its conclusions, particularly when activist organizations use them to make broader claims than the research supports. The report’s inclusion of a “dishonorable mention” list helped it generate catchy headlines and viral social media content. For instance, Greenpeace repurposed UCLA’s claims to discredit Energy Transfer, one of the companies mentioned in the report. Greenpeace, of course, failed to mention that it was found liable for claims including defamation, trespass, nuisance, conspiracy, and tortious interference for its role in the Dakota Access pipeline protests in a suit filed by Energy Transfer, the pipeline’s owner.

The UCLA analysis also overlooks a critical part of the broader picture: increased reliance on natural gas has contributed to the nation’s environmental progress. By failing to account for this contribution, the report risks misleading the public into believing that the energy companies listed are responsible for a disproportionately large share of atmospheric greenhouse gas concentrations.

U.S. energy-related carbon dioxide emissions have declined dramatically since 2005. The Congressional Budget Office has found that carbon dioxide emissions from the electric power sector have declined by about 35% since 2005. This downward trend largely stems from the shift from coal to natural gas for electric power generation. That’s not to say that reducing methane leaks from natural gas wells should not be taken seriously.

Beyond their obligation to environmental stewardship, energy companies have a financial incentive to prevent these leaks. Since methane is the primary component of natural gas, leaks represent lost product that could otherwise be sold. Insufficient pipeline infrastructure, which groups such as Greenpeace oppose, is a well-documented contributor to methane emissions from associated gas flaring, particularly in oil-producing basins where large volumes of natural gas are generated alongside crude oil.

Until that infrastructure is built to capture methane’s economic value, energy companies are taking steps to reduce their emissions. Targa, for example, has replaced gas-powered equipment with new electric compressors where practical. Over the last ten years, even as the company’s processing capacity has grown, these investments in electric compression have helped avoid nearly 25 million metric tons of greenhouse gas emissions, the equivalent of taking 5.8 million cars off the road for a year.
articles.lede: Studies masking as advocacy may drive clicks, but they don’t drive progress.

articles.title: A year of deadly floods and fires – and yet Cop31 still collapsed. When will our leaders grasp the scale of this crisis?
articles.description: Fossil fuel producers are choking off progress while we reap the whirlwind of our inaction. This is what sleepwalking to disaster looks like, says climate academic Bill McGuire
paragraphs: I t’s sometimes said that we are sleepwalking into climate catastrophe. But the reality is that we are walking into it with our eyes wide open, in the full knowledge that we are dooming the lives of our children, and countless generations down the line, to hell on Earth. In the UK, summer temperatures could hit the mid-40s within decades, making extreme drought and harvest failures the norm, and leaving people camping in the streets as houses become overheated death traps. Across Europe, the fastest-heating continent on the planet, the 50C temperature mark could be broken as soon as next year. Elsewhere, by 2050, humid heatwaves could take many thousands of lives in a single day in parts of China, South Asia and the Gulf region.

We continue to pump out the CO 2 weight-equivalent of 800,000 Titanics every year, with no end in sight. Meanwhile the latest climate Cop – the only global initiative with the potential to turn things around – has just collapsed in disarray, unable to get its act together even to agree on a vague form of words about the need to transition away from fossil fuels.

A decade ago there was some hope that we might head off the worst of global heating, when the adoption of the legally binding Paris climate agreement promised to keep the global average temperature rise to below 2C and to pursue efforts to stay this side of 1.5C. Progress is tracked on the basis of so-called nationally determined contributions (NDCs) – in other words, each country’s pledge to reduce emissions which, in the round, should mesh with the agreed temperature limits.

But the world has moved on, and not in a good way. With no binding targets or enforcing mechanisms, NDCs rapidly became decoupled from the temperature goals set in Paris. Today, even if all countries stick to their current emissions reduction policies, it is predicted that the world will still be 2.7C hotter by the century’s end, compared with preindustrial times. This in itself is a catastrophic level of heating that would mean the crossing of key tipping points, including collapse of the Greenland and West Antarctic ice sheets and the likely failure of the Amoc (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation), bringing bitter winters and baking summer droughts to the UK and northern Europe. But that “if” is doing a lot of heavy lifting, and there is no guarantee that NDCs will not be seriously diluted in the future as green policies are dumped.

So where does this leave us? The answer is in a very bad place. How quickly our world heats up is no longer only about emissions arising from our activities. The hotter the planet gets, the less carbon it is able to soak up; carbon “sinks” such as soils and forests will instead become sources that top up our emissions. Recent research suggests that by 2100, these could help pump up the heat to more than 3C above preindustrial levels.
articles.lede: I t’s sometimes said that we are sleepwalking into climate catastrophe.
