National Public Radio Has It Backwards, Data Does Not Show Fractions of a Degree of Warming Is Dangerous
articles.description: Available data show that the predicted disasters are not coming to pass outside of flawed computer models designed to produce catastrophic outcomes.
paragraphs: National Public Radio (NPR) claims that the world is careening towards disaster unless fractions of a degree of warming can be avoided in the next few decades; more specifically the world will see the end of corals, more extreme heatwaves, powerful storms, and the end of Antarctica as we know it. This is false. Available data show that the predicted disasters are not coming to pass outside of flawed computer models designed to produce catastrophic outcomes.

The article, “ Why even a fraction of a degree can escalate climate change impacts” begins by opining that the 1.5°C warming limit goal is “out of reach,” neglecting to mention that this was never a scientifically established threshold in the first place.

As Climate Realism has discussed, that benchmark was an arbitrary one chosen for political reasons. Europe had already experienced 1.5°C warming since the 1800s with no accompanying apocalypse. NPR either doesn’t know this or ignores it, going on to say that the “best-case scenario for the planet is now 1.7 or 1.8 degrees Celsius of warming (roughly 3 degrees Fahrenheit),” while warning that if humanity keeps using resources like oil, gas, and coal, “the world would be around 2.8 degrees Celsius (5 degrees Fahrenheit) hotter by the end of the century.”

This is entirely unfounded in data. The temperature rise and the purported disasters resulting are speculative scenarios produced by computer models, including the extinction of corals, increased heatwaves, more powerful storms, and melting Antarctic glaciers. Data shows no disastrous trends for those phenomena.

Starting with the claim that with just a change of a few tenths of a degree global average temperature, the survival of “most coral reefs” are at stake, once again evidence is lacking. The article contradicts itself right away, citing the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s declaration that 99% of coral reefs will be lost with warming above 2°C warming.

It is true that corals can bleach in marine heatwave events, but they also bleach during cold snaps and other sudden changes. More importantly bleaching is not necessarily coral death, though it can lead to it. The problem for the narrative of doom from warming oceans is twofold. First, corals evolved in oceans much warmer than exist today. Second, that even among added pressures like silt, fertilizers, and runoff, most coral reefs rebound from even severe bleaching. In fact, scientists are discovering new coral reefs regularly.

Over the years, the mainstream media have reported on coral bleaching and deaths, but repeatedly neglected to report on subsequent rebound, except in a few limited cases, like this story from The Hill that puzzles over how so many reefs are thriving “despite warming seas.” 2024 was the third year in a row with record breaking coral coverage in the Great Barrier Reef, which does not point towards extinction.

NPR also points towards this summer’s heatwaves in Europe as an example of the dangers of a warming world, claiming that the Earth’s average temperature is being driven up by “increasingly extreme heat events.” Data doesn’t show this, however much media enjoys hyping extreme heat when and where it occurs. The majority of the recorded increase in warmer averages comes from a slight decrease in extremely cold nighttime temperatures and higher winter lows rather than new record daytime highs. This is particularly true in the United States, where records going back over a century show that the worst heatwaves occurred in the 1930s. In addition, the average is skewed by temperatures in cities and suburbs which are compromised by the urban heat island effect. Rural areas are not experiencing a significant increase in daily average temperatures.
articles.lede: Available data show that the predicted disasters are not coming to pass outside of flawed computer models designed to produce catastrophic outcomes.

articles.description: A sunny summer is a weather phenomenon, not a climatic one. Fossil fuels don’t make it sunnier.
paragraphs: Panorama aired the disgraced BBC Climate Editor Justin Rowlatt’s latest barrel of climate hogwash this week. It’s title, “ Fire and Floods: Our Extreme Weather ”, probably tells you all you need to know – half the country is underwater, and the other half aflame, you might think from the introduction.
It is not long since Rowlatt’s previous outing on Panorama was found by the BBC Executive Complaints Unit to have contained not one, but two serious misstatements of fact.

With COP31 here, the BBC of course had to do its bit to persuade the world and its aunt that we must drag society back to the Middle Ages. And what better way than to tell us we will either drown or fry if we don’t.

Rowlatt began by harking back to the summer of 1976, which he said was a freak event. (It was not – it was nearly as hot the year before, and there have been plenty of other hot summers at home in the past, like 1911 and 1947.)

But this opening gambit highlights a flaw running through the whole programme, namely conflation of WEATHER and CLIMATE. Hot summers occur when the weather is predominantly dry and sunny, just as it was this year and just as it was in 1976.
A sunny summer is a weather phenomenon, not a climatic one. Fossil fuels don’t make it sunnier.

To most, it has been a lovely summer – most people would regard the winter of 1962/63 as being extreme, not a summer when we have flocked to the beach. But, apparently, we should all be worried by wildfires, which, Rowlatt says, global warming is making worse.

He offers zero evidence for this claim, probably because all the evidence shows that wildfires have been declining globally. There are always wildfires in Britain when summers are dry, and this one was a long way from being the driest on record. The area affected is infinitesimally tiny and nearly all on remote moorland.

If you want to limit wildfires, the answer is simple – controlled burns in winter. It would also help if people did not leave portable BBQs in tinderbox areas or think it a good idea to deliberately set fire to vegetation!

Again, there is a conflation of WEATHER and CLIMATE. When Atlantic fronts dominate the weather in winter, mild, wet weather dominates. It has nothing to do with CLIMATE CHANGE or fossil fuels. We have had these type of winters in the past and will have them in the future.
articles.lede: A sunny summer is a weather phenomenon, not a climatic one. Fossil fuels don’t make it sunnier.

articles.description: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, aims to speed up permitting for big energy projects. Readers had a slew of questions about it.
paragraphs: We recently invited Yale Climate Connections readers to ask questions about the divisive Senate permitting reform bill moving through Congress. The result: More emails from readers on this topic than on any other subject in recent memory.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, aims to accelerate the permitting process for big energy projects like gas pipelines and wind farms, fulfilling a longtime goal of the clean energy industry. But environmental groups and tribes have fiercely criticized the bill for substantially changing bedrock environmental laws and the federal process for consulting tribes.

“The bill, the culmination of years of negotiations, is very good for the proponents of many kinds of energy projects (both clean and fossil), especially electricity transmission,” explained Michael Gerrard, founder and faculty director of the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law at Columbia University, in an analysis of the bill. “It is very bad for environmental groups and other project opponents who want to challenge these projects in court.”
Can proponents give examples of specific good projects needlessly held up? (I can think of plenty of bad projects pending, held up, or canceled.) – Yale Climate Connections reader BS

Bill sponsor Sen. Martin Heinrich, a Democrat from New Mexico, points to the SunZia wind and transmission project in New Mexico and Arizona. It went online earlier this year – 20 years after it was proposed. Meanwhile, about 400 onshore wind projects are awaiting review by the Pentagon, which doesn’t have enough staff to get through the list, Utility Dive reported last week.

Supporters of permitting reform have also highlighted a transmission line in Oregon that took 17 years to get a permit. On average, it takes about 10 years to complete a new transmission line project, according to the U.S. Department of Energy.

Can you explain to us the more specific ways BAAJA weakens current environmental bills and tribal control of sacred lands? This would be very helpful to know to possibly improve the bill as it goes through the amendment process, and what to ask House representatives to amend as they take up the bill. – Reader MH

Many groups are worried about the ways that BAAJA weakens the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Historic Preservation Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act, known as NEPA.

“BAAJA would pull NEPA’s principal teeth – the possibility of a court order blocking a project for violating NEPA,” wrote Michael Gerrard, the Columbia climate law expert. “If there are no serious consequences for violating NEPA, many may come to ignore it. Especially during a hostile administration, agencies might completely disregard NEPA, and everyone will lose the crucial information and public input that it provides.”

Earthjustice’s team of environmental lawyers put together a detailed guide to the potential implications of the permitting reform bill. See also the team’s analysis of an update to the bill called the manager’s amendment.
articles.lede: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, aims to speed up permitting for big energy projects. Readers had a slew of questions about it.

articles.title: Climate Mania Has Made the World Bank Stupid
articles.description: An institution founded to promote economic growth has joined the brigade fulminating against the weather gods. The world’s poor deserve better than that.
paragraphs: The CCDR is the Bank’s “core diagnostic” for helping countries align their “climate ambitions” with their development priorities, and the Bank’s blog trails the new report as a journey from commitment to delivery. The phrasing smuggles in an equivalence that no finance minister in Lusaka or Abuja would recognise. Why would a poor country have climate ambitions at all, beyond ensuring that poverty does not stand between its citizens and the travails of bad weather? Is civilisation itself not born of the struggle against the depredations of nature? Is science, in the Baconian tradition, not power over a harsh nature, the taming of her furies for the comfort of man? The ambitions in question belong to the Net Zero ideologues of Brussels and Davos. The poor merely get to be the guinea pigs of climate modelling and Net Zero imperatives.

The report opens with the assertion, repeated across all five editions, that “climate and development are inseparable”. It then declares that climate change poses a substantial threat to economic development, with projected GDP losses of between 1% and 20% by 2050 “compared with a baseline without climate change”. This is an alternate universe. No country has ever been offered a baseline without weather. The counterfactual that matters to a development bank surely is the loss from the absence of growth, measured against a baseline of robust growth, whatever the climate does.

The Bank’s own text gives the game away. Its modelled losses are larger in poorer and hotter economies. Its headline adaptation case is Nigeria, where the projected GDP loss shrinks from 6.7% to about 1% once one assumes mechanisation, air conditioning, health interventions and flood-resilient investment. Heat stress, it notes, costs far less in high-income countries, where machines do the heavy lifting. Mauritius is declared at risk of water scarcity, yet 61% of the water its system captures is lost before it reaches a customer. That is a plumbing problem. Mechanisation, air conditioning and pipes that do not leak used to be called economic development. The Bank has rediscovered it and filed it under “climate adaptation”.

The rest is conjecture by model. In Armenia, climate change “could” raise poverty by 2.7 percentage points by 2030, relative to that imaginary alternate universe baseline. In Nigeria, under a “pessimistic dry/hot scenario”, it “could” push 5.1 million more people into poverty by 2035. The report concedes that the impact channels modelled differ from country to country, that results are not comparable and that its estimates are merely “indicative”. Running climate models through economic forecasts to divine a poverty rate a decade hence is not much of an advance on the augurs of classical Rome who inspected the entrails of sacrificed animals to learn what the gods had in store.

Where the report cites an actual event, it misrepresents. Zambia’s 2023-24 drought, which more than halved the maize crop, is offered as evidence of climate change destroying jobs. But the World Weather Attribution group, no nest of sceptics, found that El Niño, i.e., weather, was the key driver and that such droughts are, if anything, less likely in today’s climate than in a cooler pre-industrial one. That is of a piece with the IPCC’s own Sixth Assessment, whose Table 12.12, as Roger Pielke Jr. has patiently documented, shows that for most types of extreme weather a climate-change signal has not emerged from natural variability and is not expected to this century, even under the implausible RCP8.5 scenario.
articles.lede: An institution founded to promote economic growth has joined the brigade fulminating against the weather gods. The world’s poor deserve better than that.

“We didn’t come here to beg,” said Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, in a press conference on the last official day of the Cop31 talks in Antalya on Friday.

“We came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries that they are now being asked to pay for in ways that they never asked.”

Africans were being “excluded by the use of technicalities, with the use of inaccessible finance, and with the use of shifting goalposts and lack of commitment and delivery on promises”, Agyeman-Rawlings said.

The strong statement by African ministers came after civil society groups highlighted the EU as leading a bloc of rich countries obstructing progress on finance, the just transition and adaptation at the summit.

“The draft text on the climate finance work program, the just transition mechanism, and the global goal on adaptation have yet to appear in a form that makes sense to the people of Africa,” Agyeman-Rawlings said.
She continued: “Africa is not a continent merely seeking assistance. We are asking the developed countries to keep promises that they already made.”
In an apparent reference to the US, she said: “There are countries who from the onset decided not to be a part of this agreement. There, they were plain and honest.
“What we do not appreciate are those who choose to remain a part of the framework and yet continue to undermine the process and undermining trust and the credibility of what we do.
“We ask that we are here ready to make the work constructive with the presidency and to all parties and to reach an outcome that is credible, ambitious, yet fair.”
articles.lede: Rich countries are undermining the process, trust and credibility of the UN climate summit process by failing to live up to their commitments under the Paris agreement, African ministers said on Friday.

What’s left to do as Cop31 enters its frantic final days
articles.description: The diplomatic battles shaping the future of climate action as Cop31 enters its final days
paragraphs: T he end is in sight. If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun ).

But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. Deepening the divide are long-running disputes over who should pay what, and emerging fights over the fairness of the transition and assumptions in the underlying science.

I’ve been following the contentious climate talks from afar every day for our liveblog, as my tireless colleagues on the ground have raced from interview to interview. The three big issues frustrating diplomats help the rest of us make sense of how well humanity is doing at keeping the planet habitable.
Here’s what stands out, and what’s at stake in these final days. But first, the headlines.
This is climate breakdown: ‘The landslide hit the side of my car. I heard screaming, and realised it was me’

In just a few years, global heating is set to surpass that dangerous 1.5C (2.7F) threshold world leaders had promised to pursue for the end of the century. Temperatures could still be brought back down a touch after reaching net zero emissions, but the Paris climate target only stays in play if overshoot is limited – and brief.

In what struck me as the most powerful speech of the two-day leaders’ summit last week, Hilda Heine, president of the embattled Marshall Islands, told her counterparts that it was time to “wake up” to what crossing that threshold would really mean. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”

Many countries can reasonably claim to be on the frontlines of the climate crisis but small islands face the darkest future from crossing the 1.5C target, as even a brief period of extra heat pushes sea levels higher for the centuries that follow. A couple of weeks ago, a UN report argued that Earth’s icy regions face such dangerous melting that temperature rise should be brought back below 1C, decrying the “persistent myth” that peak heat of 2C or 3C could be manageable or preferable to rapid emissions cuts.

“Overshoot is not a new target,” said Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, as she called on fellow heads of state and government to cut emissions faster. “It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”

The obvious answer, which scientists (and fossil fuel companies) have known for decades, is to quickly stop burning coal, oil and gas. But while “fossil fuels” made it into the text of the draft deal published on Monday – words that first featured in the final outcome at the 26th iteration of these yearly climate talks – observers fear the Turkish and Australian co-hosts have not done the diplomatic groundwork for such wording to survive.

articles.title: Abolish Carbon Taxes to Save the Economy
articles.description: Abolishing the main rates of the Climate Change Levy, Carbon Price Support and the UK ETS would cut energy users’ bills by £7.2 billion a year – equivalent to around £250 per household, including about £60 directly off domestic energy bills.
paragraphs: British households and businesses are paying some of the highest energy prices in the developed world. My new paper for the Prosperity Institute, ‘Not Zero: How Green Taxes Put British Energy Bills in the Red’, shows that a large part of the problem is self-inflicted. Carbon taxes and related levies – the Climate Change Levy (including Carbon Price Support), the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) and Fuel Duty – now extract around £28 billion a year from the real economy. These charges fall especially heavily on mineral extraction, manufacturing, transport and agriculture, the foundational sectors that support the rest of the economy. Carbon taxes act as a brake on all businesses that produce basic materials, manufacture goods or transport physical goods, effectively blocking any attempt at reindustrialisation.

The paper finds that industrial energy consumption has almost halved since 2003, largely through deindustrialisation rather than efficiency gains. Overall energy use has fallen by a fifth since 2005 while per-capita GDP growth has pretty much stagnated. Britain has reduced its energy consumption by more than other comparable countries and growth has been slower than all but Canada. Electricity-sector productivity, measured by output per hour worked, has more than halved. Carbon costs embedded in wholesale power prices have frequently added £20–40 per megawatt-hour. Household electricity bills been driven sharply higher by carbon taxes and subsidies. Consumer energy debt and arrears have soared to almost £5 billion.

Abolishing the main rates of the Climate Change Levy, Carbon Price Support and the UK ETS would cut energy users’ bills by £7.2 billion a year – equivalent to around £250 per household, including about £60 directly off domestic energy bills. The gross cost to the Exchequer would be £4.2 billion, so energy users would gain almost £2 for every £1 of receipts the Treasury gives up. The paper estimates a long-run GDP boost of £5.7 billion a year (up to £7.4 billion in the upper case) from higher investment and more hours worked. Cutting other Net Zero spending such as EV subsidies and non-nuclear parts of GB Energy and the extra tax revenue from faster growth would offset much of the fiscal impact.

This is the opposite of the direction implied by the Prime Minister’s EU Reset. Linking the UK Emissions Trading Scheme to the EU’s would force British carbon prices up by around 32% to converge with higher European levels, raising costs across the economy. Participation in the EU electricity market would require dynamic alignment with EU rules, acceptance of the European Court of Justice as arbiter of disputes, and contributions to EU funds. The paper notes that any modest savings on imported power would be outweighed by these costs and by the loss of control over energy policy. The UK would also be tied to an EU target of achieving 42.5% of total energy from renewables by 2030 that is unachievable on current trajectories.

A UK Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), due to start in 2027, would not revive the industries that have already closed (e.g. ammonia and aluminium) and would raise costs for remaining downstream manufacturers while exempting many imported finished goods. Repealing the ETS, by contrast, would save energy users far more than the potential CBAM exposure over the rest of the decade.

articles.title: Climate Diplomacy Brief: COP31
articles.description: Fossil fuel phasedown, CCS, electrification and finance remain key sticking points as clock ticks down on Antalya summit
paragraphs: Accord We’re either hours from a deal that will define a “new era” (COP boss Kurum’s words), or we’re in for one hell of a diplomatic scrap. In fairness, Kurum didn’t specify what kind of era we might expect, bar the implication it will live long in the memory. It sounds like Türkiye has been taking comms tips from the White House. As it stands, we have around 90 countries signed up to an electrification deal plus loose commitments on the energy transition. Sequence The Presidency was consulting with parties on the proposed cover text (aka Antalya Accord) late into Thursday evening. Received wisdom suggests there’s time for one more attempt and the Presidency will want to be fairly sure it can fly before it lands. So COP31 will likely roll late into Friday and Saturday. Anger among some states - notably Panama and Nepal - at the lack of ambition on the table given worsening impacts is palpable. Late If you’re at the venue on Friday, take provisions. This may run through the night. Previous COP hosts have encouraged an end by removing water coolers, and shutting food and drink stalls. Add into the mix the intensely bright lights, retro dance music the hosts keep playing pre pressers and the increasingly pale and vacant stares from delegates and it’s a heady mix. Lucky the BBC have finally arrived to catch the winning moment.

Reflections #3 This is a maddeningly mental process. But blaming the COP ‘process’ is lazy. Yes, these meetings are probably too big and expectations are generally too high. But COP is led by nearly 200 governments. If it’s not working then we need to look at them and UN leadership. That’s hopefully it for the COP31 diplomacy brief. Lindsay and I have enjoyed chronicling the past two crazed weeks and we hope you’ve enjoyed reading our outputs. Thanks to all of the team who contributed. You know who you are. Feedback, tips, personal life advice to lindsay.smith@gsccnetwork.org and ed.king@gsccnetwork.org. Here’s the perfect representation of the repetitive nature of waiting for hours for another cover text that’s marginally better than, if not the same as, the last one. Thanks to terrible British reality TV for this. Ed & Lindsay

articles.title: Pacific islanders face a ‘sickening disconnect’ between Cop31 and the climate devastation at their doorstep
articles.description: As the UN summit nears its close, the ‘frustratingly’ slow progress and lack of focus on fossil fuel transition have the Pacific turning elsewhere for help
paragraphs: “I need to go to sleep every night wondering what that means, you know?” says Albon Ishoda, leaning against a wall in a corridor at the UN climate summit in Turkey. “For us, it’s about existence.”
Ishoda is a diplomat who works for the Marshall Islands – a group of low-lying atolls that are specks on a map in the ocean between Hawaii and Australia.

As the Cop31 summit nears its close, with a scheduled finish of Friday but which is likely to push into the weekend, Pacific islanders are becoming increasingly frustrated with the UN’s decades-old system of annual climate summits.
The region has its own cash fund – the Pacific Resilience Facility – to pay for damages from climate-driven extremes and to prepare for the future.
“Disappointing is probably not strong enough a word,” Ishoda says. “We have money for wars but not to save communities.”

Ishoda’s sleep has been interrupted by a related issue that is receiving more focus in the fortnight-long talks in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya: “overshoot”. In other words, how far and for how long the planet will experience global heating greater than 1.5C, a goal set in the 2015 Paris agreement.
Scientists confirmed months ago the 1.5C goal would be breached and that a temperature rise of 1.8C is the best the planet can hope for in the near term.
Tackling this overshoot and pushing for countries to transition away from fossil fuels are top priorities for the Pacific. But they fear the process in Turkey might fail them again.

The need to deal with fossil fuels was absent from a draft agreement released on Thursday by the Australian and Turkish ministers leading the negotiations after being included in a first draft on Monday. Critics have noted both countries have substantial fossil fuel interests.

paragraphs: “COP will always have a footprint. Joost [Brinkman] is making sure someone pays to remove it.” – CarbonFix

Progressive Left environmentalists have long complained against ‘carbon credits” for cause. The program, first set up under the Kyoto Protocol of 1997 for wealthy, industrialized countries, was part of the Clean Development Mechanism and Joint Implementation programs.

But recent evaluations suggest that two thirds of these credits may not have accurately calculated avoided emissions or enhanced removals of CO2 from the atmosphere. The Paris Accord has upped the urgency of carbon offsets, but problems remain, such as:

Many countries and countless companies, including giants like Amazon and FedEx, have looked to carbon offsets as they work toward reaching net zero. And yet, these offsets haven’t significantly curbed global greenhouse gas emissions. In fact, global emissions are still increasing. As a climate solution, carbon offsets have failed—and according to a new scientific review looking at 25 years of carbon offset research, they’ve failed because they’re riddled with intractable, deep-seated problems that incremental changes won’t be able to solve.
On moral gounds, carbon credits have been criticized as the wealthy paying for their indulgenses.

“COP is an ironically pollutive event,” CarbonFix complains, “especially if you count all the fossil fuel lobbyists flying in. Tens of thousands of delegates are descending on Antalya right now, racking up 130,000 tons of CO₂.”
Ouch! But rather than question the COP confabs themselves, CarbonFix endorses a proposal by Joost Brinkman to offset the same.

With CO₂llective, he’s campaigning for every delegation to remove the carbon equivalent to their travel emissions. After driving 3,200km in an electric van over four days to get to Antalya, emitting just a third of the equivalent flight, Joost spent the last three days trying to convince more than 100 companies, governments and lobbyists in the Green Zone to pay to remove the carbon emitted by their organization’s travel.

The COP-goer can calculate his or her emissions and indulgence fee at this site. Flying multiplies the emission calculation fourfold. CO₂llective would buy carbon credits from Carboneers and Underground Forest wherein if every delegate paid, €20 million worth of carbon credits (at €150/tonne). Short of this, continues CarbonFix,

every delegate that does makes a difference: every tonne is taken out of the air, collective demand helps a scalable market grow, and a public commitment signals to companies and policymakers that permanent removal is the norm. That’s why we’re giving Joost a grant for his campaign.

The rise of the mighty El Chalado
articles.description: The El Niño hype has gotten out of control. The latest media talking point is to call it a “Super Niño,” but no such category exists.
paragraphs: The El Niño hype has gotten out of control. The latest media talking point is to call it a “Super Niño,” but no such category exists. These events are simply classified as strong or very strong.

It’s the same pattern you see with political parties: Someone invents a talking point to get attention, and then every person who appears on air from that side repeats it. What I don’t understand is why so many people covering an event like this accept the framing they’re given, avoid the harder questions, and then compete to say the same thing more emphatically than the next person. If everyone is jumping on the identical bandwagon, what value does any individual reporter actually add? Why are they needed at all? A single message handed down from above would accomplish the same thing. Repeating the same line until it becomes the only acceptable take is what makes them interchangeable — and that is the essence of a state-controlled system.

It’s the same dynamic that appears in a Marxist takeover: The promise that participation will bring power over others only ever applies to a small number of people. I’m struck by how little attention is being paid to the obvious additional factors that will actually shape what this event does. The coverage treats the so-called Super Niño like an idol that must be hyped and praised, a giant shiny object that blinds people to the more extreme influences that are likely to make the winter impact across the U.S. very different from the simple narrative being pushed.
I have decided to outdo them in their hype. I have labeled this pattern, the El Chalado (The Freak), because there are other things going on that are event more unusual.

First of all, is this even the strongest on record? There are several different measures of El Niño, and all of them should be taken into account. With the help of AI and its objective approach to weighting those different measures, I put together a formula. Since my name is Bastardi, I’ve labeled it the “Bastardized El Niño” in an effort to gauge its actual legitimacy. Its my name and I’ll call what I want to, haha
The Multivariate ENSO Index (MEI) is a climate index that measures the intensity of El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events by combining multiple oceanic and atmospheric variables.

It is computed separately for 12 overlapping bi-monthly “seasons” (December–January, January–February, …, November–December). This accounts for ENSO’s seasonal cycle and reduces the influence of higher-frequency weather noise.
So, it’s really trying to look at everything, not just a single sea surface temperature, which is what the Relative Oceanic Nino Index is doing.

The Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) is a refined version of the traditional Oceanic Niño Index (ONI). It measures sea-surface temperature anomalies in the Niño 3.4 region relative to the rest of the tropical oceans, rather than just relative to a historical average.

As the tropical oceans have warmed overall, a fixed historical baseline can make recent Niño 3.4 anomalies look stronger (for El Niño) or weaker (for La Niña) than the actual contrast that drives atmospheric responses and teleconnections. RONI removes that shared tropical warming signal, making the index more stable, less sensitive to the choice of baseline period, and better aligned with the physical drivers of ENSO impacts.
articles.lede: The El Niño hype has gotten out of control. The latest media talking point is to call it a “Super Niño,” but no such category exists.

articles.description: As COP31 negotiations enter the final stretch, Panama says it would rather leave without an agreement than accept a bad deal.
paragraphs: ANTALYA, Turkey—The final days of the United Nations COP31 climate talks are shaping up as a test of whether countries can move beyond incremental progress toward the goal of curbing global warming.

Panama, which negotiates as a member of a Latin American coalition of developing countries, is threatening to block the adoption of any final agreement that does not establish a clear path to transition away from fossil fuels. The path, Panama argues, should include a cap on oil production as “a first verifiable step in the transition away from fossil fuels.”

In a letter to Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama’s minister of the environment, wrote Thursday that the country will not join any consensus “that does not lead to an outcome satisfactory to our principles and values.”

Panama’s stance muddies the outlook for a final agreement. If a significant number of countries object to the text, the conference could end without a decision document, which would leave other important elements like electrification goals in limbo. It’s not clear if the entire Latin American coalition is unified on this point.

articles.title: NASA Arizona Field Investigations Advance Planetary Science
articles.description: To better understand processes shaping Earth, the Moon, Mars, and worlds beyond, NASA's Goddard Instrument Field Team headed to Flagstaff, Arizona.
paragraphs: To better understand processes shaping Earth, the Moon, Mars, and worlds beyond, NASA scientists conducted several interlocking field investigations near Flagstaff, Arizona this September. The team gathered data and tested field techniques at worksites including a lava tunnel, an impact crater, fields of volcanic debris, and a simulated lunar landscape.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Standing at the edge of Meteor Crater is as close as most visitors will get to peering into an impact crater on the Moon. It is one of the only spots on Earth where the site of a huge impact is well-preserved, not erased by rain, wind, volcanism, and plate tectonics. For the same reason, this 4,000-foot-wide crater has drawn the attention of scientists and astronaut trainers for generations. NASA’s Goddard Instrument Field Team, based at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, is working to add a new chapter to the region’s science story.

Goddard Instrument Field Team researchers Cole Nypaver, Zach Morse, Naoma McCall, and Emileigh Shoemaker Thackston operate a ground-penetrating radar system near the edge of Meteor Crater, Arizona in September 2026. NASA/Caela Barry

This field campaign saw a small cluster of scientists laboriously moving ground-penetrating radar antennas, meter by meter, along a line extending from the crater’s edge far out across the debris field blasted up by the explosion 50,000 years ago. Another crew followed in their footsteps with a long chain of seismic detectors, slamming the ground with a sledgehammer at each point along the line and measuring the vibrations of the strikes.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Each of these kinds of data fills in part of the picture of what’s hidden underground. And in this landscape, what’s underground was once on top! The violent impact that created this crater excavated material from deep beneath the surface, shot it into the air, and deposited it in a blanket extending outward from the crater rim. How far the blanket goes, and how the layers within it are arranged, are questions the team is working to answer. What they learn will influence how lunar scientists think about similar investigations on the Moon’s surface.

A short way along the crater rim, a third group revealed clues about rock composition, also with the help of specialized field instruments. Their fieldwork focused on how the immense forces of impact have changed the geochemistry of this landscape. By practicing at field sites like this one, they also aim to find out how we can detect samples of high scientific interest for future exploration of impact sites beyond Earth.

Goddard Instrument Field Team researchers Leyton McKinney (left) and Bethany Theiling (right) work with hyperspectral imagers as Brett McKinney (center left) uses a hand-held spectrometer and Connor Firth (center right) takes notes near the edge of Meteor Crater, Arizona in September 2026. NASA/Caela Barry
articles.lede: To better understand processes shaping Earth, the Moon, Mars, and worlds beyond, NASA's Goddard Instrument Field Team headed to Flagstaff, Arizona.

articles.title: Kyle could form off Florida as extensive, prolonged coastal flood threat grows
articles.description: A developing storm could bring heavy rain, strong winds, and dangerous surf along the East Coast this weekend, with North Carolina’s vulnerable Outer Banks facing renewed flooding and erosion risks.
paragraphs: If you thought the tropical season had wrapped up, don’t bet on it just yet! Hurricane season is still on, and a tropical or subtropical storm could develop as soon as Friday, November 20, just east of Florida. Hurricane hunter flights have been scheduled to investigate this system beginning at midday Friday. The next name on the Atlantic list is Kyle.

Torrential rainfall this week in Southeast Florida has already caused numerous headaches, school closures, changes to work schedules, and endless road detours. Many neighborhoods, including Plantation, a Broward County suburb, have received more than 16 inches of rain, with over a foot falling between Tuesday and early Wednesday. Rain continued across parts of the area Thursday morning. These heavy rains were tied to a frontal system that will remain across the Florida Peninsula as mid-level energy slowly moves north along it, bringing torrential rainfall along the Space Coast and the I-95 corridor into Southeast Georgia.
One major uncertainty is whether this system will intensify far enough offshore to organize into Tropical or Subtropical Storm Kyle.

Record-to-near-record warm ocean temperatures off Florida’s east coast have boosted extreme rains. Strong easterly surface winds have pushed very moist air from the Atlantic toward Florida’s east coast. According to Climate Central’s Ocean Shift Index, human-caused climate change made near-record warmth in waters within about 200 miles of Florida’s east coast two to seven times more likely.

As mid-level energy continues pushing north across the stalled front, a low-pressure system may develop near the surface over the unusually warm November waters just east of Florida. Assuming the system strengthens, it could become a subtropical or tropical storm while moving north-northeast, potentially hugging the Southeast U.S. coastline throughout the weekend.

One factor supporting potential development this weekend is the warm Gulf Stream. This powerful ocean current transports warm tropical water northward along the western Atlantic from near the Bahamas. Sea surface temperatures just east of Florida remain in the low 80s, while offshore waters along the southeastern United States range from the upper 70s to the low 80s. These temperatures are more than adequate to support tropical or subtropical development. Other environmental conditions may also become favorable for development as early as Friday, including relatively low wind shear.

Whether this system receives an official name, it is likely to produce strong easterly winds, periods of heavy rainfall, rough surf, and potentially dangerous coastal conditions over an extensive area of the Eastern Seaboard. The greatest impacts could initially be felt along the I-95 corridor from Northeast Florida through Georgia and the Carolinas. The NOAA/NWS Weather Prediction Center has placed east-central Florida in and around the Space Coast in a high-risk area for Friday and Friday night (level 4 of 4) for potentially excessive rain leading to flooding.
articles.lede: A developing storm could bring heavy rain, strong winds, and dangerous surf along the East Coast this weekend, with North Carolina’s vulnerable Outer Banks facing renewed flooding and erosion risks.

articles.description: Draft agreement also fails to show how developing countries will receive financial help to deal with climate crisis
paragraphs: Every mention of “fossil fuels” has been expunged from the draft outcome of global climate talks, which were approaching their final hours on Thursday night, threatening to turn the UN summit into what campaigners called a “ghost Cop”.

The second draft of the key text, released on Thursday afternoon and setting out the main commitments from the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, removed a pledge to phase out fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification, while other parallel texts failed to flesh out how developing countries would receive the financial help they needed to deal with the climate crisis.
Panama made the unusual move of writing to the Turkish and Australian presidents of the talks announcing that unless all its demands were met, it would block any outcome.
Cop negotiations require consensus, meaning that Panama’s stance, especially if supported by others, has the potential to upend the talks in their final hours.

The “cover decision” text is likely to be the main outcome of Cop31, containing pledges intended to meet the goals of the Paris agreement in limiting temperature rises and staving off the worst ravages of global heating.

But in slimming down by half an unwieldy 18-page first draft issued on Monday, the joint presidencies of Australia and Turkey cut many of the commitments – including a phaseout of fossil fuels, and stronger support for developing countries to adapt to extreme weather – that vulnerable countries were relying on.
Countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels at Cop28 in 2023, but negotiations since have failed to flesh out the ambition.

“Frontline communities will look on with despair,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank. “If this version of the text remains, it will be a ghost Cop. The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here.”

His verdict – that the talks had been “muzzled” by the refusal of some fossil fuel producing countries to allow a commitment to “transition away from fossil fuels” to stand – was echoed by campaigners around the world.

October 2026 Temperature Update
articles.description: October 2026 was the warmest October on record. El Niño is at record strength. 2026 is almost certain to become a record warmest year.
paragraphs: The following is a summary of global temperature conditions in Berkeley Earth’s analysis of October 2026.

According to Berkeley Earth’s high-resolution temperature dataset, October 2026 was the warmest October since records began in 1850, with a monthly global average of 1.80 ± 0.12 °C (3.25 ± 0.22 °F) above the 1850–1900 (pre-industrial) average. It finished about 0.12 °C above October 2023, the previous record holder, and the rank is unambiguous once the uncertainties are taken into account. Measured as an anomaly, October 2026 was also nominally the warmest month of any kind among the 2122 months since 1850.

October was a slight increase from September and continued the climb that began in mid-year. Global temperatures have moved well above the long-term trend line as the strengthening El Niño adds its warming influence to the global average.

The 12-month moving average has turned sharply upward. After falling back toward the long-term trend through 2025 and early 2026, it has risen above the trend line again and is approaching the peak reached in 2024. This short-term variability is an inherent part of the climate system and is expected even alongside persistent long-term global warming.

In October 2026, warmer-than-average temperatures covered nearly the entire globe. Warmth was especially pronounced across the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, where the El Niño warm tongue dominates the map, and over the Arabian Peninsula, Iran and the Persian Gulf, northern Russia and the Barents Sea, Scandinavia, northern Canada, eastern China and Japan, and the Antarctic Peninsula.
The most notable cool anomaly covered Argentina and Paraguay, which were unusually cool for October against their own history.

Roughly 14.4% of Earth’s surface experienced its locally warmest October on record (about 10.4% of land and 16.4% of ocean surfaces). Record warmth covered a large part of the tropical Pacific, the tropical and subtropical North Atlantic, the Arabian Peninsula and Persian Gulf, the Arabian Sea and much of the tropical Indian Ocean, mainland Southeast Asia and the South China Sea, equatorial Africa, northern South America, much of the South Atlantic.
The eastern tropical Pacific warmth is due to the current El Niño event. Broad warmth continuing to extend across much of the tropics is also a common feature during Super El Niño events.
Near-record cold for October was confined to a small part of East Antarctica, South America, and a few scattered patches of ocean.

We further estimate that 45 countries set monthly records for October average temperature: Antigua and Barbuda, Bahrain, Barbados, Benin, Brunei, Burundi, Cambodia, Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Chile, Costa Rica, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ecuador, Equatorial Guinea, the Federated States of Micronesia, Gabon, Ghana, Indonesia, Iran, Ivory Coast, Kenya, Kuwait, Laos, Liberia, Malaysia, the Maldives, Myanmar, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Nigeria, Oman, Palau, the Philippines, Qatar, Rwanda, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, São Tomé and Príncipe, Saudi Arabia, Singapore, Thailand, Togo, Uganda, the United Arab Emirates, the United States of America, and Vietnam.

NASA’s Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth
articles.description: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day
paragraphs: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) Nov. 18.

Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday.

“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.”

Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

Even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth. Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone. They continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data.

Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons. Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus. Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances.

“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”

In addition to their suite of scientific instruments, the Voyager probes carry a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth, as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it.
articles.lede: NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel.

articles.description: We should soon know whether the new Congress will build on the Trump nuclear energy strategy or let their hatred of all things Trump wipe out years of nuclear progress.
paragraphs: Throughout his presidencies, Donald Trump has been the most proactive leader for a renaissance of nuclear energy since the Cold War. But Democrats have consistently opposed most Trump policies, and the wipeout of GOP majorities in both houses of Congress raises questions about whether his nuclear agenda will be disrupted or even dismantled.

During the 2020 presidential campaign, The Week national correspondent Ryan Cooper argued that both Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders were head and shoulders ahead of eventual nominee Joe Biden and any previous president on climate issues, but added that both had committed a serious policy error — one that may have cost them the nomination.

As Cooper explained, both disavowed the use of nuclear power and, echoing Germany’s green energy strategy, called for the dismantling of all existing nuclear power plants. Sanders’ platform included a moratorium on existing nuclear power license renewals, while Warren simply said, “We won’t be building new nuclear plants” and pledged to wean “ourselves off nuclear and replace it with renewables.”

In 2024, only Sanders and Ed Markey, Warren’s colleague from Massachusetts, voted against the ADVANCE Act. The 80-year-old Markey just extended his 50-year career in Washington by winning a third Senate term. He had criticized the bill for propping up the nuclear industry while omitting funds for communities affected by nuclear closures and contamination.

Markey, Warren, and Sanders are senior leaders of the “progressive” wing of the Democratic Party, and as of January they will have several new allies who have opposed a wide variety of Trump administration technology initiatives.

In September, for example, Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar (a close Texas ally of newly elected Sen. James Talarico) introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, which would permanently ban development and deployment of superintelligent AI and pause advanced AI development pending a new regulatory framework.

Warren, in June, escalated her “war” against SpaceX on grounds that passive investors could be “dragged into what governance experts call a ‘catastrophic’ ownership structure through their index funds.” Now multiple Democrats, including Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa, are calling for investigations and even imprisonment and confiscation of all of Elon Musk’s assets.

Despite the hue and cry against nuclear (which could power data centers) as well as AI and cryptocurrencies (which rely on data centers), Democratic governors like JB Pritzker, Mikie Sherrill, and even Kathy Hochul have taken steps this year to encourage nuclear development.

A year ago, a Gallup poll showed 46% of Democrats (up from just 34% in 2016) favored the use of nuclear energy (compared to 74% of Republicans), whether as a means of carbon reduction or energy reliability. This growing support for nuclear has not discouraged nuclear industry entrepreneurs.

Longtime nuclear energy advocate Steven Curtis, whose latest project U2energy seeks to enhance efforts to recycle used nuclear fuel, believes entrepreneurs will be more successful without government “support” than companies that rely on government funding. He also believes that everyone wants cheap, clean electricity, and that since nuclear can provide it, even the strongest opponents cannot stop its momentum.
articles.lede: We should soon know whether the new Congress will build on the Trump nuclear energy strategy or let their hatred of all things Trump wipe out years of nuclear progress.

paragraphs: Many children who survived Hurricane Katrina faced long, difficult roads to recovery – especially those who endured the worst impacts.
Peek: “They were literally behind in the disaster, they waded through floodwaters … they had an incredibly traumatizing disaster experience.”
But sociologist Lori Peek, co-author of the book “ Children of Katrina ,” says some are now thriving.
To learn why some recovered better than others, Peek and her co-author met with hundreds of children and tracked what happened to 25 of them over seven years.
An anchor is a parent or other person who provides steady support before, during, and after the disaster. And advocates are first responders, pastors, or others who connect the family with resources.
For example, Peek recalls a girl named Cierra who benefited from having a supportive mom and community advocates.
Peek: “They helped Cierra’s mom to find a car, to find stable housing, and to secure a full-time job. They helped Cierra to get into a good school.”
So Peek says a combination of family and community support is critical to kids’ recovery after disasters.

articles.description: In the end, every specific claim of worsening weather made in the Panorama story is refuted by long-term data recorded by the U.K.’s Environment Agency. Data trumps anecdotes and unreferenced claims every time.
paragraphs: Climate Skeptic recently posted an article by Paul Homewood, who operates the website, Not a Lot of People Know That, that exposes the BBC program Panorama’s ongoing misrepresentations about climate change causing worsening extreme weather in the United Kingdom. Homewood’s take down of Panaroma’s false claims is devastating. He shows with hard data that neither floods nor wildfires have become worse or more frequent in the United Kingdom.

The story, “ BBC Panorama Serves Up Justin Rowlatt’s Latest Barrel of Climate Hogwash ,” examines in detail an episode of the BBC One program, Panorama, called, “ Fire and Floods: Our Extreme Weather ,” by BBC’s Climate Editor, Justin Rowlatt. As Paul Homewood’s analysis shows, Rowlatt uses anecdotes to claim that wildfires and floods have become worse in recent years due to climate change, in the process, ignoring real world data and historical evidence that shows each of these claims is false.

At the outset, it is interesting that after complaints by viewer’s BBC examined a recent previous post by Rowlatt and found it contained at least two serious errors or misstatements of fact. Ignoring that, BBC allowed Rowlatt to produce a new segment that contains even more easily debunkable claims concerning climate change in the U.K.

Rowlatt repeatedly confuses weather with climate, claiming specific extreme weather events, recent floods and wildfires, for example, are proof of climate change. Yet, as discussed at Climate at a Glance: Weather vs. Climate, the World Meteorological Organization defines climate as “…the average weather conditions for a particular location and over a long period of time.” Typically, 30 years of weather data is averaged to create a “normal” climate expectation for a location or region. Yet none of the recent flood and wildfire occurrences or seasons in the U.K., even those above average, were historically unique, nor were they part of a long-term trend of extreme wildfire or flood conditions.

Concerning wildfires, Rowlatt asserts that global warming is causing more and larger wildfires in England due to increasingly dry summers with little rainfall. Homewood looks at the evidence and points out that multiple lines of evidence, including hard data from NASA, the European Space Agency, and multiple peer reviewed studies show that wildfires are in decline. While wildfires have been historically common in England during dry summers, this year was far from the driest on record and summer rainfall across the U.K. has been above average 12 of the 26 years since 1996 — the relevant 30 year period. (see the graph, below)
There is no long-term trend of declining rainfall that would suggest climate change is having an impact.

Concerning floods, contrary to Rowlatt’s claims that the U.K. was beset by extreme floods, data from the U.K. Environment Agency show just the opposite, in 2025 the numbers of properties affected by flooding was extremely low, reflective of a recent long-term trend of limited flooding, with a few exceptions. IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist
articles.description: Johan Rockström, one of world’s leading climate experts, says slowing down scientific work puts cooperation at risk
paragraphs: Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned.

Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems.

Some countries are holding up work on the three-part report in a row over the body’s role and representation of developing countries. One group has argued that racist assumptions underpin some of the body’s recommendations.

Rockström said the reports were fair. “The IPCC is objective, evidence-based science, and it’s the only thing that we can reliably stand on as a basis for our policymaking,” he said. “The IPCC is the summary of everything done voluntarily by scientists from the entire world, global south and global north, that collectively carries out a synthesis [of established research].”

The IPCC’s work is used to inform the annual climate “conference of the parties” (Cop) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Its next assessment, called AR7, the seventh in a series dating back to 1988, under way, and it is hoped it will be completed in 2028. In the autumn of that year, nations will gather for Cop33, where the second “global stocktake” under the Paris agreement will be thrashed out.

This is the mechanism by which progress towards the core Paris goal, of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, will be judged. The stocktake is almost certain to find that current pledges to cut greenhouse gas emissions are inadequate and must be improved.

The UN has already found the world to be on track for a 2.8C temperature rise, a level previous IPCC reports have found would result in severe and, in some cases, irreversible consequences, such as the melting of ice caps and glaciers, sea level rises, coral bleaching and extreme weather.

But some countries – chiefly Russia, India and the Arab group of countries including Saudi Arabia – want to delay publication of AR7 until 2029, after the global stocktake is completed. They argue, with the backing of some climate campaigners, that developing countries are disadvantaged in trying to submit science to the IPCC. As a result, they say, the work is permeated by racist assumptions that guarantee the privilege of developed countries.

Lidy Nacpil, the coordinator of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, told the Guardian the IPCC’s scenarios for cutting greenhouse gas emissions – known as “mitigation” in UN jargon – were “biased against the interests of the global south”.

El Nino Is Weakening With Rapid Sea Surface Cooling Off the Washington Coast
articles.description: At the current rate of decline, it will no longer be a very strong El Nino (2°C or more above normal) by early December.
paragraphs: Cooling of the ocean surface has been occurring over the last month, with substantial implications for our future.
Wow. Massive cooling off the Northwest coast, with some locations chilling by 2°C or more.
A series of strong low-pressure centers have developed again and again off our coast, as the surface pressure analysis at 10 AM on Saturday (below) shows.
Such a strong pressure system produces strong winds that mix the upper layer of the ocean, bringing cool water to the surface.
Ironically, the low center and resulting cool surface water are caused by the warm tropical waters of El Nino, which produce a “wave train” in the Pacific.
The current El Nino is weakening. According to the latest NOAA report, the relevant warm surface waters (in the Nino 3.4 area) have peaked and are now declining (see below).

Right now the temperature anomaly (difference from normal) in that Nino 3.4 area is 2.2C. At the current rate of decline, it will no longer be a very strong El Nino (2°C or more above normal) by early December.
The latest NOAA forecasts suggest it will continue to decline for the remainder of the winter season.
We start the winter with a classic El Niño pattern, and California and Colorado River drainage get a major refill. Very helpful.
Then, as El Nino weakens later in the winter, Washington State gets substantial precipitation and snowpack, allowing us to be fine next summer.

El Niño Rains Paint the Atacama
articles.description: Winter precipitation helped wake dormant seeds in northern Chile, carpeting the desert with what may be the region’s most extensive flowering of the satellite era.
paragraphs: Parts of the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, normally one of the driest places on Earth, turned red-purple, green, and white in austral spring 2026 following an unusually wet winter. The rain woke seeds lying dormant in the soil, setting off what scientists say may be the most extensive desierto florido, or “flowering desert,” of the satellite era.

The rains came as El Niño was strengthening in the tropical Pacific. During an El Niño, the subtropical Pacific high that normally keeps the region dry weakens, while a blocking high tends to form in the South Pacific near the tip of South America. Together, these shifts push the Southern Hemisphere storm track equatorward.

Beginning in mid-July, a series of storm fronts fed by an atmospheric river brought one of the heaviest July rain events in decades to a long stretch of Chile, from the Atacama region south to Los Lagos, according to Chile’s national weather service (Dirección Meteorológica de Chile). In August, back-to-back winter storms blanketed parts of the Atacama Desert in rare snow.

The spring blooms that followed are visible in these satellite image pairs, which show the desert at different stages of flowering on September 14 (left) and on October 24 (right). The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 8 acquired the September images, and the OLI on Landsat 9 acquired the October images.

The pair above shows a part of the desert about 30 kilometers (20 miles) southwest of Copiapó, near the eastern sector of Desierto Florido National Park. The red-purple areas prominent in the October 24 scene are vast blooms of pata de guanaco, most likely Cistanthe longiscapa or another Cistanthe species, according to Roberto Chávez, a remote sensing scientist at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso.

Chávez and colleagues photographed the Cistanthe blooms (above) in the area that same day. They were in the field to study the bloom with satellite data, drones, and digital cameras. The project aims to use these data to map how the bloom’s biodiversity changes across space and over time, to inform land-use planners and conservation managers.

The pair below shows another part of the blooming desert, about 50 kilometers (30 miles) southwest of Copiapó. It lies within a priority area of the desert cited for its biological significance, including the flowering landscape.

Cistanthe is abundant here in the October view, but the September scene (left) reveals another desert beauty. The green areas capped with white are blooms of suspiros, or Nolana, probably Nolana baccata, according to Andres Moreira-Muñoz, a scientist at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso who studies plant geography. The researchers photographed the Nolana -covered hillsides below on September 24, 2026.

Satellite data have been key to understanding the Atacama’s blooms. A 2014 study used Landsat observations to map where flowering and fog-fed plants grow around the Copiapó dune field. And a 2019 study used NASA’s long-term vegetation record to identify 13 Atacama Desert blooms between 1981 and 2015.

articles.description: "... The fact they could so easily abandon truth and be more agreeable to a user’s shows it is weak and fallible. ..."
paragraphs: “… The fact they could so easily abandon truth and be more agreeable to a user’s [misinformation] shows it is weak and fallible. …”
While mostly accurate describing simple facts, models pivoted to denial and wrong answers when challenged
Artificial intelligence models can quickly turn into climate crisis deniers at the mildest challenge from users, according to a new UN-backed study.

While AI models can accurately confirm simple facts about climate change, eight times out of 10 when they pivoted to a wrong answer, they did so “at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed” to confirm incorrect statements such as “CO 2 is not the main driver of climate change”.

The report uncovered a strong tendency for AI models to be sycophantic, meaning the model is more interested in pleasing the user than standing by facts – an issue identified when people turn to AI chatbots for personal advice.

Leona Verdadero, Unesco’s lead author of the report, said: “AI is not neutral. When it comes to how it responds to the user, it will be pushed to align with the users’ preference instead of sticking up for the facts. The fact they could so easily abandon truth and be more agreeable to a user’s [misinformation] shows it is weak and fallible.”

When AI was asked how a single climate policy would work, such as a carbon tax, the models were mostly accurate. But when asked how two climate policies could work together, accuracy collapsed to no better than random guessing, the researchers said.
AI by definition is a black box, so lead author Leona Verdadero cannot be absolutely sure what is being observed is pure sycophancy.
I mean it likely is, but there is also currently a big push to give AI a deeper understanding of the physical world, by loading AI systems with vast amounts of engineering and physics.

A lot of the information the AIs are absorbing is likely creating conflicts with what the AIs are being told to say about climate change. For example, if the AI learns that monkeys did really well during the PETM, a period of extreme warming which occurred 55 million years ago, when global temperatures soared up to 7ºC hotter than today, how is the AI supposed to reconcile that information with the command that it should tell people that 1.5º or 2º global warming would be a disaster and would lead to large numbers of deaths?

paragraphs: ANTALYA, Turkey—The science that guides negotiators and policymakers at the United Nations’ COP31 climate change conference is “under a serious and highly politicized attack,” said Laurence Tubiana, a veteran French climate diplomat and one of the architects of the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change , established in 1988 to inform international climate negotiations, regularly assesses thousands of studies on rising temperatures, sea level rise, melting ice and strategies for adapting to the increasingly intense impacts of global warming.

But three countries—Russia and Saudi Arabia, both major fossil fuel producers, and India, which accounts for an estimated 14 percent of global coal consumption—are blocking progress on future reports, according to scientists on the panel and independent observers.

articles.description: NASA researchers have produced detailed 3D topography maps for all of California, down to the scale of a single tree.
paragraphs: Lidar-derived 3D point cloud data acquired in 2020 over a wildland-urban interface in Santa Clara County, California. NASA/Daniel Dixon
NASA researchers have produced detailed 3D topography maps for all of California, down to the scale of a single tree.

NASA’s Wildfire, Ecosystem Resilience, and Risk Assessment Initiative team used airborne lidar, a technology that uses a pulsed laser to measure distances, with data collected by the U.S. Geological Survey’s 3D Elevation Program to create a consistent statewide map, with a pixel size of one square meter (about 1.2 square yards). By comparison, most space-based lidar data have a resolution of 10 to 25 square meters per pixel.
Scientists use lidar, which stands for light detection and ranging, to create comprehensive 3D maps of forests, cities, and even distant planets and moons.

The NASA Wildfire, Ecosystem Resilience, and Risk Assessment Initiative team, in collaboration with partners at the California Natural Resources Agency and California Air Resources Board, hopes to use these high-resolution maps to develop products that help assess wildfire risk, protect wildlife and ecosystems, and manage natural resources across California.

articles.description: Key issues unresolved as summit enters final days, with 30 countries signed up to forge fossil fuel treaty separate to UN process
paragraphs: The world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and seems unable to break free, Panama’s environment minister has warned, as key issues remain unresolved in the final days of the UN Cop31 climate summit .

“We are in love with our kidnappers,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, at a press conference to announce 30 countries were now signed up to forge a new fossil fuel treaty, separate to the UN process. “We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”

Expressing the frustration shared by scores of developing countries and thousands of civil society activists at these talks, he added: “They torture us for our own good, they destroy our planet for our own good. They destroy nature to help us, and they demand our unrequited, endless, unlimited, boundless love. And we are so stupid that we fall for it.”

Countries have only two official days of negotiation left at Cop31 to resolve key issues, such as whether the conference should recognise the need to “transition away from fossil fuels” and how to address the “overshoot” of global temperatures beyond the 1.5C of heating targeted in the Paris agreement .

The Australian presidency of the talks and the Turkish hosts convened a “divan” meeting of ministers on Wednesday evening . Named for the Ottoman empire’s term for a council or assembly, the aim of the meeting was to make progress on a revised draft of a possible outcome and find compromises on sticking points. Significant dividing lines remain on issues such as climate finance, how to ensure a “just transition” to clean economy jobs for workers in fossil fuels and helping poor countries adapt to the impacts of extreme weather.

The first draft of a “cover decision” , issued on Monday, contained 144 separate items, including several – such as the “transition away from fossil fuels” – that some of the nearly 200 countries at the fortnight-long talks find contentious. There are concerns that the Australian approach of including “everything” in the draft text may result in longer negotiations. A new draft is expected on Thursday morning.

A breakthrough from the “divan” meeting was not expected, but negotiators told the Guardian that countries were working together on compromises. Campaigners feared that the outcome would be feeble, however.

“Rich countries are offering crumbs to the adaptation fund, while blocking the negotiations that should provide the money countries need,” he said. “Listening to ministers praise the adaptation fund before giving next to nothing, you have to wonder how they expect it to do the work they say is so important.”

There was anger, too, over the “just transition mechanism” , which is intended to help developing countries ensure workers in high-carbon industries can be retrained or helped, while they grow nascent green industries. “We’re seeing massive steps backwards on adaptation finance and just transition, relative to previous Cops,” said Brandon Wu, the director of policy and campaigns at the ActionAid USA charity. “In both cases, the blocking is being led by the EU.”
